subtopic: ARTICLES OF ILLITERACY-SOUTH AM NEWS CONGRATULATED
ARTICLES OF ILLITERACY-SOUTH AM NEWS CONGRATULATED

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we begin today to debate the 1987 constitutional accord I wish to add my voice in support of this initiative of our Government. I believe it is the most significant accomplishment of our mandate.
Our Party's political agenda has been one of national reconciliation, and we have not strayed from our course. In 1984 our Leader promised to improve relations between Ottawa and the provinces. As Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), with this achievement, he has done just that. He has strengthened our federation and revitalized our national unity. The Prime Minister and the 10 Premiers should be highly commended for succeeding where others have failed.
Canadians across the land have welcomed Quebec, and with it one of our nation's founding cultures, back into the constitutional family. As Members of this federal institution our participation in ratifying this accomplishment is indeed historic. I wish to thank our Leader for providing this significant opportunity, and for an enormous deed well done.

subtopic: CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATE SLASHED BY CANADA TRUST
CREDIT CARD INTEREST RATE SLASHED BY CANADA TRUST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last month several credit card companies increased interest charges on unpaid balances. Today one company, Canada Trust, announced it will slash its rate to a record 13.5 per cent. Its cards will not carry any annual fee, transaction charge or monthly statement cost. In effect, credit card balances will become like consumer loans.
If one company can do this, why can't others? This company will make a profit at 13.5 per cent. It is not a charitable institution. We ask, therefore, why must other MasterCard issuers charge 18.9 per cent? Why must VISA issuers add annual fees and transaction charges to their 16.5 per cent rate? Why do leading retail stores charge 28.8 per cent?
The House has given first reading to a Bill that will protect consumers against excessive interest charges. If one major trust company can push rates down to this historic low let no lobbyist tell any Member of this House that rates have to be so high that only an alpine climber can reach them.
September 29, 1987

subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS-TRADE DEFICIT WITH PACIFIC RIM COUNTRIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS-TRADE DEFICIT WITH PACIFIC RIM COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister with regard to trade. Since his Government came to power Canada's trade surplus with the United States has fallen by half. Our trade deficit with the Pacific Rim countries is five times worse than when the Prime Minister assumed office. Imports from Europe are growing four times faster than are our exports from Europe. Believe it or not, Canada's trade deficit with Japan, the world's second largest industrial power, is 24 times worse than when the Prime Minister came to power. Talk about lost opportunities.
In light of the Government's truly pathetic record on worldwide trade would the Prime Minister bring this House up to date on recent developments in his obsessive desire to get a free trade deal with the United States? What did the Americans offer yesterday? What are Canadians conceding today? What is the stage of these negotiations?

subtopic: STATUS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES TALKS-TRADE DEFICIT WITH PACIFIC RIM COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian trading patterns remain strong and buoyant around the world. There has been a great deal of work done.
In fact, I know my right hon. friend will want to reflect upon what he said inasmuch as he was a member of an administration which talked about a third option-reducing our dependence on the United States. When that was begun in 1972, 65 per cent of our exports went to the United States. When it ended, 80 per cent of our exports went to the United States.
Rather than reducing our dependence there was a complete failure on the multilateral side by the Liberals, which brought about a situation in which it is clearly in the national interest to seek a comprehensive framework for such a large part of our foreign trade.
The trade talks have been complex and challenging. There was an important review yesterday. That review is ongoing further to a report of the Minister of Finance and the Minister for International Trade. At the earliest possible moment I will report to my right hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I want to address some supplementary questions, if I might, to the Prime Minister. He has just acknowledged that a trade deal of this comprehension is complicated, difficult and complex. Mr. Speaker, I suppose the effective trade strategy is the one like the Liberal Party introduced in 1972 where we did not increase multilaterally. Our dependence on the United States increased directly as a result of the lack of policy of the Liberals, and it is because of the enormity of the problem that we are trying to seek to preserve jobs in Canada and create others by a comprehensive framework which will lend stability and security to the trading relationship.

The Prime Minister has still not answered the fundamental problem, that is, you have got five days to go. You have got a negotiating process-

All I can say to the Hon. Member is that we have put into the legal aid system, by virtue of agreements put forward for the next three years, record amounts of money to be made available to areas which are essentially under provincial jurisdiction. If the previous Government had had only a particle of the commitment to legal aid that this Government has, I would have been the first to congratulate it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question has, of course, arisen in the course of negotiations with the provinces. There is an element of flexibility in these agreements to allow for cost recovery, in appropriate cases for which legal aid has been provided, from those people who are indeed in a position to contribute. This is a matter that has nothing to do with Party affiliation. For example, in the Province of Ontario where, as my hon. friend will know, there is a Liberal Government, there are provisions whereby moneys can be recovered with respect to the delivery of legal aid. All I am saying is that we are setting down as a basis of the discussions we are having on an ongoing basis with the provinces fair and reasonable propositions with respect to cost recovery.
If there are individual cases, we want to make sure that they are followed in accordance with the agreement we have entered into with the provinces. In terms of actual commitment, this Government has increased substantially the amount of money contributed to legal aid across Canada. I think the Hon. Member should be the first one to acknowledge that and to give us some acclaim for that action.

CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 Constitution Act, 1867
1.	The Constitution Act. 1867 is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 1 thereof, the following section;
"2. (1) The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with
(a)	the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and Englishspeaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada; and
(b)	the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society.
(2)	The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a) is affirmed.
(3)	The role of the legislature and Government of Quebec to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in paragraph (l)(b) is affirmed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock p.m., the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, on September 22, one week ago today, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) if he would facilitate a meeting of women's constitutional experts and government constitutional advisers to examine the impact, if any, of the constitutional accord on women's equality rights. The Prime Minister facetiously dismissed the question, as did the Canadian Press.
Today the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women made a similar request, enlarging it to suggest that there be a national conference convened for the purpose of seeing if there is any case to be made for women's equality
rights and other equality rights, including that of minorities, having been put in jeopardy. I urge the Prime Minister to look very seriously at this request and not just shrug it off as he did my earlier request. He should facilitate the holding of such a national conference.
I also urge him to pay some attention to the report of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitutional Accord. I was really shocked this morning when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) made no reference to the recommendations of that committee. It is as if all the work we did during the summer, all the witnesses we heard at our hearings, all the recommendations they made to us, were for nought. The Minister simply ignored the report. He probably has not read it, but he could have at least tried to have read the last chapter.
Since no other Minister of this House was involved in the process of drawing up the Constitutional Accord, I think all of us would expect the Prime Minister, in preparing himself to speak on the Accord, as I am sure he will, to very carefully study the recommendations of the joint committee concerning aboriginal rights, particularly self-government, and the unfairness of the Accord to the people of the North.
Indeed, there is a very strong recommendation that there is no justice for the exclusion of the territorial government's nominees to the Supreme Court and that the unanimity rule for the entry of new provinces is much too constraining. It is recommended that linguistic duality be promoted as well as preserved, that there be far more attention paid to the ethnocultural reality of Canada, and that the First Ministers should give serious consideration to the possible repeal of section 33 of the Charter, the over-ride section, which is of particular concern to minorities in the country. It is recommended that there be a process of Charter reviews since it became so clear during the hearings this summer that many aspects of the Charter itself are questionable. In some ways we are having a good deal more trouble with the Charter than with the Constitutional Accord itself.
Finally, we hope that the Prime Minister will at least address the question of the process of constitutional reform of which the Minister made no mention at all this morning. Apparently the Minister thinks that the process of the First Ministers getting together to draw up an agreement and consulting the Canadian public only after it had been done was just dandy.
The Special Joint Committee makes a very powerful recommendation that there be a permanent joint committee of both Houses on constitutional reform and renewal which would hold hearings across the country before the First Ministers meet on such matters as equality rights, the ethnocultural reality of Canada, the over-ride clause of the Charter, and the aboriginal peoples' rights to self-government.
September 29, 1987

It is recommended that we encourage the Canadian public, as well as the constitutional experts and professional associations, to participate in those hearings and that they be funded to do so. We cannot go on forever expecting volunteer groups to take hours and hours of their time preparing learned briefs without any payment for their efforts. We must, therefore, have funded participation. As a result of this process specific recommendations can be made to First Ministers so that they will know what is of most concern to Canadians with regard to constitutional reform.
I hope there would be some indication from the Prime Minister that attention has been paid to this and other recommendations of the joint committee. I would ask also that they read the New Democratic Party addendum. I spoke at length this morning about our concerns for the equality rights of women and our amendment in that connection. My colleagues will be speaking of our amendments already foreshadowed by the joint committee report with respect to fairness to our northern citizens and fairness to aboriginal peoples. They will be speaking in the course of the debate on those proposed amendments.
Finally, I want to reiterate that saying yes to Quebec after Quebec said yes to Canada in the referendum is one of the most exciting achievements that we have known in this generation.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to say how pleased I am to be able to participate in this historic debate and to have been able to sit on the committee. The joint committee of the House and the Senate studied the Meech Lake Accord and heard from a number of witnesses. I will come to my conclusions about the witnesses in a moment, but I cannot refrain from putting forward the point which witness after witness put forward, that is, that they needed more time to do a proper job.
The Meech Lake Accord is an achievement which I support for reasons that I will remind the House of in a moment. However, it could have been much better if the Government had been generous with it, if the Government had held hearings to give the people a true opportunity to put forward their opinions.
In spite of the committee hearings we experienced today what can only be referred to as executive federalism, that is, the changing of our Constitution basically by action of the executive of Parliament, the executive branch of the federal Government, and the executive of the provinces. That is not the way in which the Constitution should move forward.
My colleague, the Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), spoke about the joyous occasion which she thought this ought to be. In many ways it is, but how much better it would have been if the Government had been generous toward the people of Canada and given them every opportunity to prepare their brief in the amount of time
Constitution Amendment, 1987
they needed and to present them. Even more important, the Government should have given the people of Canada the hearing that they deserve.
I can say as a member of the committee who was present from beginning to end that there was never any intention of the Government to listen to the people of Canada. The Minister who was responsible for the matter, Senator Murray, indicated that they were only interested in hearing about egregious errors. They were not interested in hearing about ways in which the Accord could be improved. They were not interested in hearing about things which could be added to the Accord to make it a document which would have the support of a much broader constituency. That was not of interest to them. Their interest was only in technical errors in the work of the executive at the federal and provincial levels.
I am disappointed in both of those features. I am disappointed because my own conclusion and that of members of my Party who sat on the committee and listened to the witnesses is that it is a step forward, it is an Accord that we should support, but that it could have been a better opportunity for our country. It could have been an opportunity to address concerns of a number of constituencies which could have been addressed without in any way taking anything from the achievement represented by the Meech Lake and Langevin agreements.
A number of criticisms were made of the agreement. There are criticisms of the idea of a distinct society, criticisms of giving the provincial Governments any role at all in the composition of the Supreme Court, and criticism of the way in which Senate reform is to be brought forward, hopefully, but not necessarily, on an urgent basis, much to our regret.
However, by and large the amendments, and certainly the amendments to which the Official Opposition has loaned its support and which we have signed, are amendments which take nothing away from the fundamental achievement of Meech Lake which, as I have indicated, merely-if I can use that term-clarify it in a number of areas in which clarification is in order and add to it by bringing to the Meech Lake Accord the support of a number of groups which feel left out.
I would like to indicate why the Meech Lake Accord has my support. Our Leader spoke this morning of the very important achievement of bringing the Government of Quebec back into the process of negotiating further changes in our Constitution. I understood, and perhaps some Members of the House do not, the circumstances that in my view made it impossible for the Government of Quebec to have approved of the patriation and Charter in 1982. Even if the Meech Lake Accord had been presented by the Government of the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, I do not think it would have been acceptable to the Government of Premier Levesque. Therefore, I am one who looks at that period as one where unanimity was not obtainable.

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
In the present circumstances, unanimity has been attainable and has been attained. The mere bringing of the Government of Quebec back to the table in constitutional evolution assures that there will be further evolution of our Constitution or, at least, that there can be. Without Quebec at the table we could have reruns of the kinds of sad failures that occurred with the native self-government initiative where, with a certain measure of goodwill on the part of the parties who participated, it was still impossible to work out a satisfactory agreement.
In the future, when we talk about Senate reform, an elected Senate, as I hope we will, and when we talk about the possible redistribution of powers between Section 91 and Section 92, about strengthening the Canadian economic union, and when we talk, as I hope we will, in future constitutional discussions about removing the notwithstanding clause so that no legislature and the Parliament of this country can deliberately pass laws which defy the Charter and to which the Charter is not applicable, Quebec will be there.
When all of that constitutional agenda; native rights, the recognition of the multicultural community in Canada, things that were not done in this round of constitutional negotiations, are discussed Quebec will be there, and that to me is a substantial achievement. It is an achievement which makes the Meech Lake Accord worth supporting and my leader indicated all of that.
I think it is also important to indicate that Quebec's adherence and support was not achieved at a cost of weakening our country. It was not achieved at a cost of making what has been wrongly referred to as the most decentralized federal system in the world-which our system is not-an even more decentralized system. 1 have studied the Accord. I have heard the witnesses. What I like about the Meech Lake Accord is that it does not do these things.
If one remembers, back in the early 1970s governments and spokespersons from Quebec had a pretty heavy list. They wanted to take control of the CBC within the borders of the Province of Quebec. They wanted to take over the communications power. They wanted a strong and specific power in the area of international relations. They wanted to license radio and television broadcasting stations and cable companies. They wanted the responsibility for the situation of the francophone minorities in other provinces of our country. These were matters which were in the past on the agenda of the Province of Quebec under former governments. They were matters which would have led to a Quebec within Canada with a very special status.
In my opinion, special status is one thing that is not a part of the Meech Lake Accord. A weakening of the federal Government is not a part of the Meech Lake Accord. As I look through it, I see that Section 91 and Section 92 which allocate powers to the two levels of Government are unchanged. Not only are they unchanged, but specific language is put into the Meech Lake Accord to make it absolutely certain that nothing
is to be taken away or added to either level of Government's powers under Section 91 and Section 92. That is there specifically. That applies, of course, to spending and to fund raising, raising money by various means of taxation. It is unchanged in the Meech Lake Accord. Both levels of Government retain all the powers they had before without gaining anything and without giving anything away.
I am particularly happy as well that the concept which the former Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, brought forward in the Official Languages Bill in 1969, enhanced as we continued in terms of constitutional amendments in 1981 and 1982, is unchanged. Bilingualism, as we conceived it back in 1969, is if anything strengthened in the Meech Lake Accord. It is not strengthened as much as I would have liked, but it is marginally strengthened. The door is open and I hope it will remain open for us to strengthen it in the future.
For example, Section 23, which provides for instruction for minority language communities across the country where numbers warrant, is still there. We in the Liberal Party called for the removal of that condition "where numbers warrant". We wanted a more generous attitude toward the situation of official language minorities across the country, whether English or French. I regret to reflect that, from what we understand, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and the federal Government did not even ask for such changes. No suggestion was made to the provinces that "where numbers warrant" should be removed. However, that provision is there and it is strengthened marginally, as I indicated.
The Meech Lake Accord puts an obligation on the provincial Governments and the federal Government to preserve the linguistic duality of our country. Not only is Section 23 still there to continue to protect the official language minorities, but the Official Languages Act itself is still the law of the land. The provision is still in the Constitution whereby any province can declare itself to be officially bilingual, and where citizens' rights are enhanced in whichever province that occurs.
One opportunity was lost by our whole country through the Prime Minister's failure to raise that issue, to try on the occasion of the Meech Lake Accord to enhance the opportunity by seeing another province or another two provinces recognize officially their bilingual character. In our amendments, and the Liberal Party policy, last November, we called on Canada to move further along the line of provinces being officially bilingual. Nothing was done about it. However, as I indicated, I do not see the Meech Lake Accord as taking anything away from the type of official bilingualism that was begun by the Trudeau Government and which continues to be a national commitment.
Another thing that makes me pleased about the Meech Lake Accord is that the national leadership of the federal Government continues, in my view, to be a national possibility. There is still room with the powers the federal Government has, with peace, order and good government which is not diminished,
September 29, 1987

with the undoubted power, clarified, of the federal Government to spend money in areas of exclusive provincial responsibility, hedged, admittedly, by a provision contained in the Meech Lake Accord, but recognized that there still is an opportunity for the federal Government to provide national leadership.
I think there is a certain confusion in the country about that subject. 1 do not think the federal Government is providing national leadership now. I think we have a federal Government that is withdrawing from its role of national leadership. One could see from the daycare program the Government proposed that it is not interested in providing national leadership in national programs. One can see from the answer the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) gave me not one half hour ago about legal aid that the Government is not interested in providing national leadership. One can see in the environment, in consumer protection, in the cries of our cities for support for urban infrastructural costs, that the Government is not interested in providing national leadership.
But that is a very different thing from saying that the evolution of our Constitution deprives the federal Government of the opportunity to provide national leadership. I think the way in which we will have national leadership from the federal Government is to defeat the present Government and to elect a Government of a different political colour, for instance, a Liberal Government.
No!

The Hon. Member from the New Democratic Party complains. Let me just say that I think that if an NDP Government were elected, the Meech Lake Accord would not be an obstacle to it in exercising national leadership.
When one looks at the Meech Lake Accord one should not hold it against the Accord that we have a federal Government that has copped out of providing national leadership in many, many important areas of life in Canada. That is this Government's style. It is a style that has won it the low position which it now holds in Canadian public opinion.
In our minority report we introduced a number of amendments. I think that it is accurate to characterize these amendments as clarifications and as additions. I cannot see them being characterized or considered as derogations from what was achieved at Meech Lake. I honestly believe, and it is the position of our Party, that it is not too late for these amendments to be considered by the Governments of Canada, provincial and federal, that have not yet taken the final steps that would make this Accord part of our Constitution. If that were done and if the list of amendments were considered and adopted, how could anyone argue that they would not improve the Meech Lake Accord?
The best the committee could do in its majority report was to come to the conclusion, not that the Liberal amendments
Constitution Amendment, 1987
would take anything away from the Accord, but that they could not be achieved, that there would not be the will or the consensus among Governments to make such changes. That is speculation by government Members, perhaps directed by the Government House Leader or the Minister responsible for this measure. I have more faith than that in the possibility of these amendments being adopted.
The amendments are not supported by us alone. These amendments have tremendous support across Canada. There are amendments dealing with multiculturalism, putting the question of native self-government on the agenda and dealing with the entry of the territories into provincehood. Each one of our amendments is an amendment that has tremendous support across the country. They take absolutely nothing away from what was achieved at Meech Lake. I want to urge Members of Parliament to reflect on that point.
There are now a number of Liberal provincial Governments in the country. It is a reasonable question to ask what the federal Liberals feel the provincial Liberal Governments should do. In speaking for myself I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the last thing we would want from any Liberal Leader or Liberal Premier is for them to say, "Well, 1 have read the Liberal amendments in the minority report and I have changed my mind about the Meech Lake Accord. We will only support it in this province if the other Parties agree to the minority Liberal report that was just put out in Ottawa". That is the last thing that we want. We want the Meech Lake Accord to go forward. What we are hoping is that Premiers and, indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), will look at our list, consult with their colleagues and reflect on the fact that these amendments do not diminish the achievement of Meech Lake but that, in fact, they enhance it. They bring to it the support of many groups that now feel out of the process, that feel they are not part of it. I think these amendments can be achieved. I urge them on all Hon. Members.
I hope that procedures will be developed in this debate for us to be able to present each of our amendments for the consideration of our colleagues. I would like to see Members of the House vote against the amendments. How could they vote against the recognition of multiculturalism as a fundamental characteristic of our country? Or how could they vote against the idea of an elected Senate? I name but a few, Mr. Speaker.
I want to conclude by asking Members to look at the amendments, not the weight of them, not their number, but for what they each stand, and for what they would do to make the Meech Lake Accord a better deal for Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions, comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay).

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure and a sense of privilege and honour that I rise today to support the Meech Lake Agreement now before this House.

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
One of the witnesses who came before the committee, the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau, recalled that in 1930 Parliamentarian Henri Bourassa noted that in Canada there were an Ontario patriotism, a Quebec patriotism and a Western patriotism, but no Canadian patriotism and that there would be no Canadian nation as long as there would be no Canadian patriotism.
Like Mr. Trudeau, I find that essential, Mr. Speaker, and 1 propose to assess the various clauses of the Accord in the light of what Bourassa called-and I am referring here to Henri Bourassa-Canadian patriotism. But Mr. Trudeau was wrong because clearly there is a Canadian patriotism, but we must go out and tap that patriotism instead of staying in Ottawa and calling for it.
Mr. Speaker, allow me in my preamble to refer briefly to my roots and explain the starting point in my assessment. My family was in Manitoba before Manitoba entered the Canadian Confederation. My parents came to St. Boniface during the 40s from a small Manitoba village named Sainte-Anne-des-Chenes. I would point out to you that in a province where the majority language is English, my parents did not speak that language. So I, as a youngster learned very soon in the street what it meant to belong to a minority group, when my first language was French and all my friends spoke English only. I soon learned also that in Manitoba teaching French was not allowed. I vividly remember that when the school inspector came to visit our classes, our French books and crucifixes had to be hidden away. French was taught nonetheless but it was against the law.
Later in life, I had an opportunity to represent Canada to the University Hockey World Games in Turin, in 1966. And there, for the first time, I noted that the world does not always perceive us as we see ourselves in Canada. The translator who was provided for our team only spoke Italian and French, because it was taken for granted that all Canadian hockey players were French-speaking. I also felt for the first time what it means for a young Canadian to walk behind one's flag and to experience the emotion felt for this wonderful country.
So I view that Accord as a fancophone from outside Quebec, as a very proud Manitoban and as a Canadian, and I state as clearly as I can that it is not impossible to be a threefold patriot. Only the weak are afraid of a distinct society. Only the weak wish everybody were alike in Canada.

I come to the House to speak in this debate as a franco-Manitoban, as a westerner. I can only say to you, Mr. Speaker, that for westerners Ottawa is pretty far away. We know that it is far away because we cannot drive to it in one day. We know that our National Arts Centre, our House of Commons and our Government are located in Ottawa, and we know that they are all far away. We know what happened when a purported national Government passed a national energy plan and struck the Foreign Investment Review Agency. We know that these
instruments have the capacity for removing the capital that we westerners require to develop ourselves.
This morning the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) mentioned conflict and confrontation. In western Canada we know a great deal about conflict and confrontation. For a long time we have felt that this is what our national Government was doing to us.
When I look at Meech Lake, as Mr. Bourassa has stated, I speak of a Canadian patriotism. I know it is possible to be a Manitoban, a franco-Manitoban, and a Canadian, and that one does not exclude the others.
When we started our work as a committee this summer the first thing that was said to us was that our committee was a sham and a rubber stamp. Because I wished to be sure that all of the questions of my constituents were put on the table, on the first day I asked the Minister responsible what was the hurry with this process. Had the federal Government sold the farm? What was the purpose of the committee? I asked those questions, and I can stand before you today and state that I asked them because I wanted the answers, and I received the answers that I wished.
I know today that these were the wrong questions to ask. They were not the questions that mattered. People talked about the process being a sham. Of course, hindsight is the best teacher we have ever had. Looking back we might suggest a different process for the next round. The committee did exactly that.
When people talk about a process to avoid substance, I am reminded of the preacher who wrote in the margin of his speech for Sunday, "Weak point, shout louder". Process is one consideration, substance is another. The substantial agreement of Meech Lake is far more important than the process that led to it.
When people talk about federal or provincial power, my constituents remind me regularly that who provides which service is less important to them than the fact that a quality service is provided. They do not wish us to fight about power. They wish Governments to deliver the services required.
When the media criticizes this Accord and the process, I know that the committee would wish me to say to them and to the other critics that we wish they would read the letters from the 301 people who wrote in to us, the testimony of the 100 or so witnesses who appeared before the committee, and the complete analysis of the committee's report. We have not only put forth our recommendations for all to see, we have put forth the analysis which led to them. Critics should pass the test of agreeing or disagreeing with our analysis and not with some superficial vision that they read in the newspaper.
The Accord allows Quebec to resume its full role in the Canadian constitutional family and thus repair the damage done to national unity when Quebec was isolated in 1981.
September 29, 1987

After the referendum, former Prime Minister Trudeau promised renewal. What Quebec got was an agreement in 1982 which did not reflect the renewal that they sought. The Accord respects the equality of the provinces, assures federal authority in the capacity to exercise national leadership. It fosters co-operation and reinforces the federal structure of Canada.
It is that vision of Canada that I wish to support. This vision does not see a strong federal Government and weak provincial Governments. It does not see winning and losing, but rather it sees all Canadians and all Governments working together in the best national interest.
One question that we asked ourselves was, should we reopen the Accord? We concluded that it was the unanimous agreement of 11 First Ministers, all of whom are committed to proceeding with its ratification, that those 11 Ministers represented us, and that it would be our decision as a Parliament to agree or not to agree. In our view, opening up the Accord and considering amendments would have led to pressure to reopen the Accord for other subjects. There is no guarantee that, if we were to reopen this Accord, the necessary consensus could then be restructured on a different set of objectives.
Further, there is no pragmatic reason to reopen the Accord, since many of the changes being sought will be easier to accomplish in the future when Quebec sits as a full and participating member for constitutional renewal. There is no morally justifiable reason to reopen the Accord. I wish to remind all Flon. Members that, unlike a number of those groups seeking changes, Quebec was left isolated, and again may be left isolated.
I support the suggestion that we must look at aboriginal selfgovernment. It is very clear that we wish to do that. Need I remind Members that we have had four such conferences and they all ended in failure? Merely saying that another conference should be held is not sufficient. All of the participants must rework their positions and seek a solution.
There is no question that the deliberations that led to more discussion and concern on our part was the matter of the Charter of Rights. We came to the conclusion, based not only on our own opinions but on the opinions of countless witnesses who supported that position, that the distinct society clause will not take away, override, or supersede Charter rights. The courts can now take into account the reality of Quebec's distinct society, where relevant. Quebec's willing acceptance of the Charter's legitimacy strengthens the Charter itself and the values it reflects.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, for a franco-Manitoban like myself, constitutional recognition of the existence of French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians in this country marks a decisive step in our history, as does confirmation in our Constitution of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the role of Parliament and of each provincial legislature to protect this fundamental reality.
Obviously, some people will want us to go even further. Suffice it to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had put on the table the promotion of minority rights throughout the country during these discussions and that there was no concensus at the time.
Our Government is now sponsoring a Bill on official languages. I believe that it will soon become law. We are making some progress, and the Committee itself recommended that this major issue of the promotion of minority rights be put back on the table.

Senate reform will be the first item on the next round of constitutional discussions. I believe that Senate reform will occur. What is more important, I disagree with the suggestion of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition this morning that he would prefer returning to the seven provinces or the 50 per cent majority for this item. The committee disagrees. I need not remind Members that under that formula the two large provinces and five others could tell my province or the Province of Alberta what type of Senate reform they would have. We believe that to be inappropriate. There will be Senate reform, and there will be an elected Senate, but it will be the type of reform that is supported by each province in Canada.
All through the summer the committee met, with the participation of all Parties. It worked long hours, it heard at least a hundred hours of testimony from witnesses who gave this subject incredibly close consideration despite all of the comments on the process being hasty. These Canadians had obviously thought about this a great deal. They cared a lot about the subject. They wished to present their views to us and to all Canadians.
The committee's report stated that the question before Parliament and therefore before us in preparing this report is not whether a different solution might have been reached, or whether other constitutional issues might also have been addressed. Clearly the answer is yes to those questions. It is quite simply whether or not the Accord that has been agreed upon should be adopted, or whether any amendments should now be adopted.
The evidence heard by the committee suggests that the terms of this Accord reflect a compromise. No one should expect perfection in a compromise. A number of witnesses told us that the provisions of the Accord as it is now constituted are the absolute minimum terms upon which it will be possible to secure agreement among the Government of Canada and the provinces including Quebec not only now but into the foreseeable future.
It was under this opinion, which was reflected by most of the witnesses, that we recommended adoption of the Accord.

September 29, 1987
Adjournment Debate
There were as always-and there will be here in the House of Commons-a number of worse case scenarios put forth. If these assumptions had been accepted by the committee, it would be appropriate to reject the Accord on that basis. If the worse case assumptions were the appropriate criteria, one would have withheld legislative power from the provinces over property and civil rights out of fear that it could be used to expropriate all private land holdings.
The committee looked at the worse case scenarios. Dean John Whyte of Queen's University Law School gave us a test in which we could address them. It was as follows: "Therefore the deficiencies of the Accord must be serious and they must be likely". As a member of the committee I say to the House that the critics have not met their own test. The deficiencies of the Accord are not serious and they are not likely.
The committee will now deal with the future of constitutional change. The British North America Act was not written as a constitution for all of us as modern Canadians. It served us well, and the repatriation of 1982 was important to Canada. In the future the process can be improved. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms should be looked at again, because questions are being asked about its application. Residents of Yukon and the Northwest Territories should have the same rights as other Canadians in respect of having candidates for the Supreme Court. Aboriginal self-government must be on our agenda. The promotion of our linguistic duality must be on our agenda. The ethno-cultural quality of Canada must be on our agenda, as well as a reformed Senate and the fisheries considerations.
These do not in any way detract from the Meech Lake Accord. They are things which we as Canadians have determined that we want to look at in terms of our future Constitution.
In conclusion, I want to make some comments from the point of view of a westerner who has seen conflict and confrontation. I think I came here partially because I wanted to bring to Canada a new sense of civility. Partisanship, yes, and disagreement, yes, but based on principle not on power. It is not who wins or loses. It is not the central power or the federal power versus the decentralized or provincial power. Canadians are residents of their provinces and they are Canadians. They do not want to fight over power. They want services provided.
It is not whether the Senate is appointed by the federal Government or the provinces, although it is clearly reasonable in our state to have the provinces being given a say in appointments to the Senate. What Canadians have been telling us is that they want an elected Senate. However, until it is elected, it seems reasonable that both groups would be represented.
Also it seems reasonable that judges should be appointed in consultation between the federal Government and the provincial Government. After all, the umpire of Confederation should be chosen by both teams.
It is not whether shared services are paid for by the federal Government or the provincial Government. I remind everyone that there is only one taxpayer. That taxpayer wants services provided and does not want his or her resources wasted by a fight over who is to deliver the services.
The findings of the committee really addressed themselves to a serious analysis of the following question: Is this Accord a good deal for Canada? In our report we addressed sequentially all the considerations. We stated our analyses and we gave our recommendations.
I think the committee has said-and I want to say it to the House-that the Accord is a great act of national reconciliation. It makes the country whole again. It is not flawed, as some say. It has its imperfections and its deficiencies. It points out a number of other national concerns which need to be addressed. It can be improved. The Constitution can be improved. The process of constitution-making needs to be improved. The substance of constitutional change needs to be addressed.
I came to the House of Commons in 1984 with a feeling about Canada which reflected my roots as a francophone outside Quebec, a minority member of this great Canadian country; as a Manitoban and a westerner who felt that confrontation and conflict had taken over where working together ought to be the norm; and, above all, as a Canadian who felt that this country in all its parts was a magnificent place in which to live, one of which we were all proud.
The Meech Lake Accord is not a perfect document for all times. It accomplishes its major objective, that of bringing Quebec into Confederation and of making a better Canada for all. I recommend to the House of Commons its adoption with all due speed.

Mr. Speaker, I should like in the first place to congratulate the Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) for the excellent speech he made in this House a few minutes ago.
Mr. Speaker, today we are having this historic debate in the House just like the historic debate we had seven years ago on the patriation of the Canadian Constitution.

I recommend very strongly to Members of the House the report of the joint committee which talks about not only the things that must be done today in terms of the Meech Lake agreement but also some recommendations for the future. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will look very seriously at the recommendations we are making not only about the Meech Lake agreement today but about future constitutional change, about what should be on the agenda, and about the fact that we are recommending a joint committee of the House and of the other place on an ongoing basis for constitutional discussion. These are very important matters.
We had a broad consensus of the three political Parties in attendance at the meetings this summer. I was very proud, along with the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), to be a member of the committee and to see the consensus among all three political Parties.
Before rising to speak today, I went through some back editions of Hansard and came upon the one for May 22, 1980, two days after the national referendum in Quebec. At that
Constitution Amendment, 1987
time the New Democratic Party had an opposition day, and I was the constitutional critic for my Party. We had an opportunity to put the following motion before the House:
That this House welcomes the result of the referendum in Quebec and
pledges itself to interpret that vote as a clear call for constitutional change.
I am very happy to say that I think all three Parties recognize that back on May 20, 1980 the people of Quebec voted yes for Canada and yes for constitutional change. I think the Meech Lake agreement will provide that major constitutional change and will bring Quebec, in the constitutional sense, back into the Canadian family. I believe that is very important.

Seven years ago, Quebec said yes to Canada in a referendum and now, Mr. Speaker, we have the opportunity to say yes to Quebec and we should do so. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec's National Assembly passed the Meech Lake Accord three or four months ago. Could 1 now vote against Quebec? I am proud also to be from the first Englishspeaking province in Canada that passed the agreement last week in Regina, that is Saskatchewan, my native province.
Another quite significant fact, Mr. Speaker, is that now the three federal political Parties are in agreement. We have 11 First Ministers who agree on the Meech Lake Accord.
I think that is really significant.
I would like to go back over the history of why it is so important to have Quebec back in the Constitution, back in the Canadian federation in the constitutional sense. We spent some 25 years talking about what kind of a constitutional arrangement Quebec wants. We spent a lot of political energy on that question over the last quarter of a century.

I remember quite well the quiet revolution in Quebec during the sixties with Mr. Lesage as Premier and other important people such as Rene Levesque. There were two or three others who were also important at that time. Afterwards, there was Daniel Johnson's election campaign with the theme: "Independence or equality." He won the election with such a platform. Then there was the Victoria Conference in 1971 where a constitutional agreement was signed by all Premiers but then Mr. Bourassa who was Premier, on his return to Quebec revised his position. There was still some constitutional confusion afterwards.
During that period, the Parti Quebecois with Mr. Rene Levesque was founded. I very well remember November 15, 1976, and I think that all Canadians, all Quebecers well remember that date, November 15, 1976, when Mr. Levesque won the election with a huge majority in Quebec, forcing the goal of national independence for the people of Quebec. After that there was the May 1980 referendum. That was a tough

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
moment for Quebecers, and not only for Quebecers but for all Canadians across this great land.

We spent much political energy and much energy in general trying to come to terms with how Canada is organized. We now have an historic opportunity to have Quebec in the Confederation constitutionally, and L say, let us not miss that opportunity.
This afternoon, I would like to read the words of one person who appeared before our committee, and I will do so in English because I think it is a very important message for those of us who are English-speaking Canadians. It is the testimony provided by Madam Solange Chaput-Rolland. For me, she was the most moving witness who appeared before the committee. She appealed to those of us in the other nine provinces to understand how badly needed is the Meech Lake Accord. She said:
I think none outside Quebec knew the reality of the referendum. I travelled throughout Canada, about a few months after. It was all over, eh? Good. It was not exactly all over. Families against families, towns against towns, fathers and mothers not speaking to their children.
(During the Referendum) we spoke with thousands of Quebeckers. Women wanted to leave their children a country as big as the one they had received from their father. That was mainly the article that reached the heart, because you are right: in this country if we put a little more heart into what we are doing, maybe we would be aware of the hurt we inflict on others.
And then we came home. We went back to the National Assembly, back to our villages, back to our houses, back to the friends that were no more friends; they were on the "yes", we were on the "no". It was not a picnic, it was not a social gathering, it was not a think-tank, it was a battle between brothers, a dangerous, divisive battle, and we still feel it. It was not 100 years ago, it was seven years ago that we lived that referendum.
English Canada could not care less one month after, and it stung me and it stung all of us who fought so hard to remain in Canada and to find ourselves outside of Canada. You know, it was a very dramatic gesture when Mr. Levesque put the flag of Quebec at half mast on the day you were all celebrating here.
But our hearts were at half mast too that day, because we were out of a country we had chosen to remain.
So the Accord of Meech Lake brought us something "incroyable" as a gesture of friendship-
And I would really like people to know that for us Quebeckers, as for all the others here and everyone else, the Meech Lake accords are not an end, but the beginning of a grand process, I think. But I must tell you that for me it is really the first time that I have felt, YES, I won that referendum.
But surely by now, surely, you all know that if Meech is to fail for whatever reason, there can be no more negotiations, no more justifications.
If Quebec is once again to realize that it is more difficult to opt in Canada than to stay out of Canada, then surely, you know that the roads of tomorrow can only lead to another form of independence, but this time not chosen by any political party in Quebec, maybe chosen and imposed on Quebec outside Quebec.
I believe the testimony of Madam Chaput-Rolland was very moving. I think the time has come when we must say yes to Quebec and make Quebec once again part of the constitutional family.
I also want to say that we as a Party very proudly support the idea that Quebec is a distinct society within Canada. This
resolution says that Quebec is a distinct society within Canada as it is the only province with a French-speaking majority and an English-speaking minority. It is very much a distinct society.
As a Party, we also support the concept of linguistic duality as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. Those are very positive reasons for supporting the Accord.
Aside from the Quebec reasons for supporting the Accord, there are other reasons as well. As I said before, we spent some 25 years on the Quebec question. One of the other reasons for supporting the Accord is that once Quebec is part of the constitutional family, a log-jam or a blockage that had existed will have been broken. Once Quebec is part of the family, we can begin to address seriously many other questions of constitutional change and build a Constitution that is even better for all Canadians from coast to coast.
As the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam said, the Meech Lake Accord also deals with co-operative federalism. She described the co-operative federalism of the 1960s under Mr. Pearson and the great confrontation and divisiveness of the 1970s and the early 1980s under Mr. Trudeau. Once again, this Accord is one that is built on a philosophy of co-operative federalism, and that is good for Canada. That is reflected in the way Supreme Court Justices are now to be chosen. The provinces will have a chance to nominate or recommend people for the Supreme Court, and the federal Government will have the final say by choosing from the list.
The Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam also mentioned that spending powers are now enshrined in the Constitution for the first time. From our point of view, that is a very positive thing. The opting out with compensation is a positive thing for Canada and it reflects the Canadian reality.
I do not think that any of the social programs that exist today would not be in existence if this particular formula had been used previously. For example, I would remind the House that when medicare came in, only two provinces agreed to it, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. Ontario was opposed to it. There was no medical care until there was a national will to have it and until the federal Government started putting in big bucks toward making medical care a reality.
The Quebec Pension Plan is another example of opting out. It is a very good pension plan and in some ways is even better than the Canada Pension Plan.
Also enshrined in the Accord is the equality of provinces. To me, a person who comes from a small province with a million people, that is very important in my vision of federalism.
Those are the positive things about the Accord. That is why, even without amendment, the House should vote overwhelmingly in favour of the Accord so that we may go on to build a tremendous country.
September 29, 1987

There are some ways to improve the Accord. In its addendum, our Party has suggested three specific, logical amendments that could be used to make the Accord even better. The amendments do not detract from the Accord nor do they unravel it. Indeed, they build on the Accord and make it all the better.
The first is fairness in the north. It is beyond me why the First Ministers would treat people north of 60 differently from the way they treat people south of 60. The people in the north do not have an opportunity through their territorial assemblies to nominate people to the Supreme Court of Canada or the Senate. I call upon all the First Ministers, including the Prime Minister, to change the Accord to make sure there is no discrimination against those people. This would not detract from the rights of people in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia or anywhere else but it would make the Accord all the better.
In my opinion, the 11 First Ministers also did a very bad thing in changing the amending formula to require unanimity for the creation of new provinces. That is not fair at all. In 1905, my province came into Confederation in an arrangement made between it and Ottawa. In 1949, Newfoundland came into Confederation in an arrangement between it and Ottawa. That was a bilateral process and did not affect the other provinces. Why change it now?
As a compromise perhaps we should stay with the existing amending formula brought in by Pierre Trudeau in 1981-82 which says you can create a new province if you have the support of seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population. That is a compromise which would not be as discriminatory against the north.
Second, we suggest fairness for the aboriginal people of Canada. We suggest that conferences on native self-government be enshrined in Section 50 of the Accord. We are now putting on the agenda in the Accord itself conferences on the Senate and the fishery, and I appeal to our First Minister in this House to go back to his colleagues and try to persuade them to enshrine the obligation of aboriginal rights conferences within the Meech Lake Accord itself. That does not detract from anyone's powers or rights. In fact, in my opinion it adds to our rights and fulness as Canadians to make sure that we discuss Indian self-government at First Ministers' conferences very soon.

And, finally, Mr. Speaker, we also recommended and proposed justice for Canadian women. This morning, my colleague from New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) took up several minutes to deal with the necessity of having it in Section XVI, where reference is made to multicultural groups and the native people of Canada. We must also mention Section XXVIII of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and refer to Canadian women and have total
Constitution Amendment, 1987
enshrinement of equality rights for both men and women in Canada. That is so important, Mr. Speaker, that I wonder why the eleven First Ministers overlooked such a right that is basic to Canadian women.

There are a number of other things one can mention. In our addendum we say it is very important for future agendas that we undertake a Charter review. Once again, my colleague mentioned the interaction on women's rights between Section 1 and Section 15 and Section 28. We certainly support the process of review. We also want to mention the override part of the Charter, Section 33, which should be reviewed, particularly when it comes to equality rights. I personally think with respect to discrimination on the basis of sex or colour that there should be no override whatsoever. We should not be able to legislate the removal of those kinds of rights. The override refers to many other things as well and I think we should be reviewing everything that it touches.
The second point referred to in our suggestions for the future is to flesh out the Canadian family in a more real sense. We have to look at recognition in the Constitution of the future of the ethno-cultural reality of Canada as a fundamental characteristic. Over 30 per cent of Canadians have backgrounds which are not Anglo-Saxon, francophone or native Indian. I suppose half my family background, given my Swedish name, reflects that ethno-cultural reality. The time has come to try to create the political will to recognize as soon as possible in future rounds the ethno-cultural reality. I know with your ethno-cultural background you would certainly be in agreement with having the First Ministers discuss this as soon as possible after the Meech Lake Accord is resolved.
I see you bending over in your chair in enthusiasm, Mr. Speaker, but I have one last point to make and that is on the process.

He is a good man, Mr. Speaker, a good MP, the Hon. Member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) who belongs to the Ukrainian ethnic group. I come from what is perhaps the most Ukrainian constituency in Canada, the constituency of Yorkton-Melville. That proposal is just as important to you as it is to me, Mr. Speaker, and you will agree on that.

We suggest and underline what is said in Chapter 15 of this report. We have to democratize the process. Constitution building is for the people of Canada, not just for 11 First Ministers, not just for bureaucrats and not just for Ministers in charge of the Constitution. In fact, it is not just for MPs or MLAs or MNAs. It is for the people of Canada. One way of doing that is by supporting the recommendation for a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, an ongoing committee to make suggestions to First Ministers on constitutional change and hold hearings across this country.

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987

Public hearings are so important for Canadian men and women, and I hope the other Legislative Assemblies, in Saskatchewan and everywhere, will do the same to provide a more democratic process for having constitutional changes made here in Canada.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, we have a great land.

We have a historic opportunity to bring Quebec into the Canadian family constitutionally, and once we do that we will have an even greater chance to make some of the changes I have talked about for the future, that is for the ethno-cultural reality, women, and the aboriginal people.
Mr. Speaker, it is time we did something.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments. Debate. The Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier).

Mr. Speaker, as a Quebecer and as a Canadian it is with emotion and pride that I rise today to support the historic accord of last June 3. First allow me to emphasize the vision and sense of history which inspired our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who was the great artisan of this accord. But each provincial Premier as well had to show much courage and selflessness to reach this accord. Indeed each provincial Premier had to demonstrate a particular feeling for the state and ignore personal and immediate interests to achieve this historic compromise which enables Canada to become whole again and Quebec to resume its role of consenting and henceforth active partner within the Canadian federation.
What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is an example of political courage, and we all know that such gestures in politics are few and far between. This is why the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial Premiers who signed the accord will be highly regarded by the historians of this country.
The debate we are launching today in Canada's Parliament comes on the heels of lengthy negotiations. The process was difficult, sometimes painful. And I experienced these debates, first as a Quebecer, as a Canadian in Ottawa and then in Quebec. I too must admit that I had doubts at times. I was not sure whether Quebec might one day be able to achieve selffulfillment without repudiating any aspects of its own personality in the Canadian Federation. We were being asked the question in a dramatic way: Was it possible to fully experience our pride, that of our roots, of our mother tongue and of our French culture, and at the same time to be just as proud to be Canadians? How could that be reconciled with the remembrance of our French ancestors who were lost in this hostile territory and who, gradually, traveled through the whole continent and eventually settled there only to lose it again, and the oppression from which conquered people generally suffer?
How could we preserve a language and a culture which stemmed from our roots and associate them with the reality of a country to be built, a mostly anglophone Canada to be called our own? Many decades were to go by before one day those realities could be reconciled. Indeed, had it not been resolved in some quarters that the Canadian citizenship required absolutely and without qualification the reduction of this other reality that is part of the soul of a people: its language, its culture, its tradition?
It is about that dilemma and the sufferings it has caused throughout our history that I want to talk about, because it is not futile to view the Meech Lake Accord in a historical perspective. In fact, history recounts the anguish, the conflicts and ultimately the achievement of having remained what we are: French speaking people in Canada, on the American continent.
The history of this people that Mr. Trudeau, when he just recently appeared before the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, the history of this people that Mr. Trudeau described as a small people speaking a little understood dialect, is the history of a handful of French men and women isolated in a snowy land. In short, 60,000 people who had a dream of occupying a whole continent. That history is made of struggles, of shattered hopes, of extravagant dreams and bloody rebellions, but above all it is made of pride, a pride that is rooted in continuance, the pride of having survived in spite of all opposition and throughout all the misadventures that abound in our history. The pride of having maintained our language and our culture for more than two centuries and of being able to come here today in this House to assert in French our pride to be French speaking Canadians. That is what our Prime Minister was talking about in his speech delivered in Sept-Iles in August, 1984. Quebec men and women, said he, love Quebec and are proud to be Canadian. But Quebec men and women also love Canada and they are also proud of being Quebecers. They have a big enough heart for both loyalties. There is no doubt what has guided our Prime Minister and the Premiers of every province of Canada who have made possible on June 3 last, thanks to their ability to compromise, the return of Quebec in the constitutional family by signing the Meech Lake Accord.
A renewed federation had been promised to those among Quebecers who bet on Canada on May 20, 1980, which was the day of the Quebec referendum. However, a yes for Canada was also a no to certain things. It was a no to a uniform Canada governed from Ottawa where Quebec always seemed to be the loser. In his speech in Sept-Iles, the Prime Minister also stated: "One thing is certain, no Quebecer authorized the federal Liberals to take advantage of the confusion in Quebec after the referendum to ostracize their province from the Constitution." Mr. Mulroney also said: "My Party is not happy about the political weakening of Quebec caused by the unfortunate events which have taken place in Canada and in
September 29, 1987

Quebec. If Quebec is weakened, all Canada is weakened. If Quebec is strong, all Canada is strong. One of the component of this yes to Canada was the reassertion of the distinctive character of Quebec society and its right to be different within the Canadian federation."
On May 21, 1980, the day after the Quebec referendum, Mr. Trudeau assured us that renewal of federalism was possible. Not only was this renewal possible, but also desirable, according to him. Not only was it desirable, but also achievable, and in the very near future. After believing this promise, Quebecers were surprised to learn in 1982 that the Canadian Constitution would be repatriated. This took place without the agreement of Quebec and more or less behind its back. Experts have told us that the Constitution Act, 1982, was imposed to the Quebec Government against the will of the Legislative Assembly.
Quebec was therefore legally committed to the Canadian federation, but against its will. The Supreme Court recognized that this was unconstitutional. Moreover, many Quebecers added that it was immoral. In practice, this created two Canadas: A Canada made up of nine English-speaking provinces which had adhered to the Constitution, and a Canada composed of one francophone province, Quebec, which had not.
Can we now say no to Quebec, as the Liberal opposition in this House is doing? For all practical purposes, the Liberals are ready to sign the Meech Lake Accord, but they are also proposing a series of amendments which would simply destroy this Accord. Naturally, this is in line with the policy of the Trudeau Government, and the same people are now telling us the very same things in 1987. But the motto of Quebec is Je me souviens, and Quebecers do, indeed, remember.
Mr. Speaker, we shall not see the aspirations of Quebec rejected once more. We shall not now have the rest of Canada ask what Quebec wants and refusing to hear the answer.
It would actually be extremely dangerous to open up this Accord which is rather flimsy. Flimsy it is because it implies a certain amount of renouncement on the part of several provincial representatives who have signed this Accord. Flimsy it is also because, if we open it, each of them might see this as an opportunity to return with his shopping list, with his probably legitimate demands, but which are far from being as urgent as Quebec's return to the Canadian fold. Now, I should like to quote one of the key witnesses who appeared before the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, namely Professor William Letterman, the former Dean of Law School at Queen's University. He said: "It is our view, Sir, that it would be very dangerous to start amending this text at this point. As I have said, this is an extraordinary operation to repair an unfortunate omission in 1982, and it responds to what the Quebec Government has told us would satisfy them. We think that objective is so important that we do not want to see it jeopardized in any way". It is neither I nor a member of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
this Tory Government who is saying that, but a former Dean of Law School at Queen's University.
As members of the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, we were overwhelmed very early with this feeling of urgency and felt the need to'correct this historical mistake as soon as possible. In the light of this historical urgency, we were mandated to study the Meech Lake Accord to ascertain whether there were in it any weaknesses, such as exist in any other constitutional agreement, which might be contrary to the letter and the spirit of the Constitution. We could not find any. We found a number of clauses which could be improved upon, and that is why we have made a number of recommendations for future constitutional conferences.
It would be clearly out of the question to try and repair an injustice by creating other injustices against other Canadians or groups living in this country. But the nature of Quebec's distinct society which we have recognized had already been taken into account in a number of Supreme Court decisions as well as in our history. I should like to quote again from the statement made by Professor Letterman before our Joint Committee: "Nevertheless, I think it has been true since 1867 that the courts have known that the Quebec society is, in certain important ways, a distinct society." As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the concept was not new. The idea was first and foremost to make room for a sociological reality. "That has always weighted with them in settling constitutional issues that touched closely on Quebec. This has been implicit." And Professor Letterman added: "I believe it is worth making that which has been implicit explicit, in general terms, because it is, as we say in our brief, one of the fundamental realities of the Canadian free and democratic society, and has been from the beginning".
But we had also to take into account the flimsiness of the Accord. And that is what we did for several weeks last summer.
We have examined the Accord with our hearts, with open minds and in a spirit of accommodation. We have heard many groups. We have heard people tell us what they fear, what they worry about and what they want changed. Our review was rigorous and straightforward and each aspect was scrutinized with all due respect for those who had accepted to come and share their problems with us. But in the final analysis, we have not found in this historical compromise any obvious flaw which would frighten anyone in Canada. And those who fear that we may embark upon the slippery slope of the two nations concept must recognize along with Professor Letterman that nothing has changed, since Quebec's distinct society and unique character have been acknowledged on many occasions since 1867. It is therefore in a spirit of joy and pride that the provinces have greeted Quebec as an active member of the great constitutional family.
Mr. Speaker, we must be proud to support the first ministers' accord and to strive to make Canada a country where

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
belonging does not mean being the same and where living is worthwhile.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend a question. With respect to the very careful deliberations she says they undertook in committee, and I appreciate the time, effort, consideration and concern that was part and parcel of a very important aspect of our life here in Canada, I wonder if the Hon. Member would explain to me the interpretation of Article 91, their questions and answers with respect to minority francophones and the consequences-

-the legal consequences of linguistic duality. Could she explain to me what the following part of page 52 means, and I quote: The Joint Committee accepts the advice that the "linguistic duality" clause is a constitutional step in the right direction for French-speaking minorities outside Quebec and that in law the "distinct society" clause is unlikely to erode in any significant way the existing entrenched constitutional rights of the English-speaking minority in Quebec.
Could my colleague explain what the committee means when it says the clause cannot in any way diminish rights.

In a sense, could she explain the intent of "the clause is unlikely to erode in any significant way the existing entrenched constitutional rights"? What is "a significant way", and how would it be diminished or not?

Mr. Speaker, 1 believe the whole report is very clear on that point. The distinct society in Quebec exists since 1867. It existed under another crown, the crown of France, then under the crown of England. That has not changed in any way. My Hon. colleague will recognize that the English-speaking people in Quebec have always enjoyed a privileged situation as a minority in Canada. But sooner or later Quebecers had to assert their French culture. They had to convince everyone in Canada not only that they were able to defend their language but that their language, that of the majority, had to be spoken in the workplace, to be the current language and allow Quebec to affirm itself as different.
I do not think the English-speaking minorities in Quebec ever had to fear the loss of their language. Over the years they were given two universities, numerous services in their own language, and McGill University, for instance, is certainly one the finest of all Canadian universities. But the six million French-speaking Quebecers are lost on a continent of 225 million English-speaking people. We must not mince words. It is obvious to me the English-speaking minority in Quebec will survive with the support of the 225 million English-speaking
who inhabit this continent, and will survive regardless of the French fact in Quebec, as it has always survived and asserted itself through the years.

speechtext: I would like to ask my Hon. colleague what grounds she has for saying that at Meech Lake, and I quote: "The Liberals said no to Quebec". I would like to know what she means when she says about the Meech Lake Accord that the Liberals said no to Quebec, for in my humble opinion the Liberals said yes.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to answer this question because many editorial writers have dealt with it in recent weeks. The hypocrisy of the current Liberal Opposition has been pointed out. I think it is very clear. On the one hand, they say yes, the Accord has their full support and, of course, they will not question it, but on the other hand they bring forth amendments. The list of amendments, if you analyse it, contains items that are so important that to all intents and purposes they are tantamount to questioning the Accord.
What I am saying and repeating in this House to my hon. colleague, and I speak as a former university professor, is that when in a text there are so many things which in one's opinion are offensive and objectionable, it would seem that the only thing to do is not to sign the text. However, the Liberals want to win on both sides, as they have always wanted to do.
