I appreciate it, Mr. Speaker and I thank my colleague. I did not know that the microphones were not working. I am sorry about that. As the technician of the Official Opposition, I am responsible for certain things in my Party, but not for the microphones or the sound system.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, I had to vote against the 1981 Agreement in spite of the fact that I was for patriation and for inclusion of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and that I was happy that linguistic guarantees would be entrenched in the Constitution in Sections 16 to 20, as well as in Section 23 which guaranteed the minority language educational rights of the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec and the English-speaking minority in Quebec.
However, the wording of these clauses did not go far enough to preserve and promote minorities, and left too much to the interpretation of the courts. Hon. Members may recall that I clearly stated a few times in the House that the adoption of such a Charter gave very great powers to the courts compared to those traditonally given to this House, and I cautioned the Members of this House, at least generally, that they should be very certain that they understood exactly what this Charter of Rights and Freedoms meant.
Certain provisions of the 1981 Charter were too restrictive. For instance, the words "where the number is sufficient to warrant" in Section 23 left a bitter taste in my mouth as a French speaking Member from Ontario who is himself part of the linguistic minority. I deplored the absence of Quebec and I deplored the notwithstanding provision in Section 23. I also deplored at the time the fact that, in my opinion, the majority had not shown to this minority, which is important for the very existence of Canada, the generosity necessary to allow it to develop throughout Canada, which I consider essential for the survival of a Canada with two official languages.
I would now like to recall some of the arguments raised at the time. Hon. Members will remember that amendments had been suggested both by the Conservative Party and by other Members of this House. The debate was quite lengthy and certain amendments were accepted. I know, for instance, that Section 23 was rewritten partly because of some comments made by Members of this House. I was one of them. I do not take all the credit for this, but I do say that we had the benefit of a Government and of First Ministers who were willing to listen to our views.

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
It will be remembered that in my opinion the quantification of rights was not an acceptable concept. People have or do not have rights. If one requires justification in order to exercise one's rights, there is a great danger that many people will not exercise such rights. They will bow before the will of the majority, the easy solution, and will be assimilated. This is what is happening in this country.
Minorities need support from their leaders and politicians. Minorities should not always have to fight in order to exercise their rights, because this gets to be tiring, and very draining in the long run. Minorities should not need to be always on the defensive; this is why it is important that the Canadian Government, my national Government, not only ensure the protection of minority groups in Canada but promote those groups. This is essential for this country. Again, calculating my rights, quantifying my rights is something mean, and one is forced into a beggar's position. That is not a healthy attitude because it emphasizes the role of the dominant group versus that of the dominated one. Language equality in Canada is a concept that is not tied to the reality of numbers. We say that French and English are the two official languages in this country and that they have equal status. Therefore, any quantification of basic rights to existence in this country and to our language rights that are so dear to us must be eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, the 1982 Constitutional Agreement also stemmed from a political compromise. Indeed, Prime Minister Pierre Elliot Trudeau told me in this House, on January 29, 1979, in answer to a question concerning the rights to language equality to be included in the Constitution via the Charter, and I quote:
I would insist on the fact that this bill of rights should and must include a
bill of rights protecting official language minorities all over the country.
However, in 1981, we found ourselves tied to a document that did not entirely tally with that declaration of intent of the Prime Minister. There were loopholes as I said in the protection of minorities, and Canada became in that respect a mosaic in which minority rights varied and still vary according to the province where you live. In each of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, there is a different situation. Of course there was Quebec, Manitoba, New-Brunswick, where constitutional protection existed. And there were the other ones, where if numbers warranted it, certain privileges were granted. But language rights, constitutional rights as such did not exist for the minority group. Also, in the 1981 Agreement Quebec was absent.
For all those reasons, I took a negative stand, as I had to do in conscience, Mr. Speaker. At that time, it will be remembered that my constituents and certain Members in this House well understood my position and did not blame me for taking it, even though at times it was to them an embarrassment and
a source of difficulties. At that time, in November 1981, I situated my argument within the following conceptual framework. I am quoting from Hansard, p. 1336, a speech that I made. One should not quote oneself, Mr. Speaker, but I think this will sum up my thoughts so I can move to another matter. I am quoting:
The main purpose of a constitution is to guarantee the rights of citizens beyond the reach of any political power. Furthermore, it should not be used to protect the right of majorities but rather those of minorities, for the former, the majorities, protect themselves naturally through their numbers, through political influence and through the environment they create. That is why protection of the rights of the minorities cannot be left in the hands of the majorities, nor in those, for that matter, of the various legislative assemblies.
Today in 1987, six years later, I wish to set my intervention in the same context and analyze the Meech Lake Accord in the light of constitutional safeguards to protect language legislation for minorities, that is, French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec and English-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
Today, six years later, contrary to what I did in 1981, I will vote, Mr. Speaker, for the constitutional arrangement agreed upon in Meech Lake, for the Accord stemming from the Meech-Langevin meetings. However, the critical analysis that I intend to make and put forward about minority rights will prompt me to discuss an amendment that was proposed by my party, the Liberal Party.
First of all, I would like to briefly recap what is contained in the Meech Lake Accord and discuss what is new about it. The first question that comes to mind, Mr. Speaker, is the following: Why the Meech Lake Accord? The answer is obvious. This accord is the result of constitutional discussions that were initiated at the time of the patriation of the Constitution in 1981 and that were pursued ever since with the aim of putting an end to the constitutional isolation of Quebec. The Meech Lake Accord fulfills this goal and I do not know a single Canadian who is not happy about it. This adhesion of Quebec to the Constitution is a fundamental achievement that will condition my vote and I know that several of my colleagues will vote with me.
In a climate of mutual understanding and of fraternity, the federal government and the nine other provincial Governments have demonstrated at Meech Lake their attachment to Quebec and Quebecers. For that, they must be congratulated.
But who in fact took the initiative? Was it the federal Government or the provincial legislatures? Neither. The Accord has its origin in a document that was prepared in Quebec in June, 1985, in the manifesto that was published by the Quebec Liberal Party under the title Maitriser I'avenir.
That document outlined the five propositions that Quebec deemed essential for joining the Constitution. I would like to briefly review them:
September 29, 1987

1)	The explicit recognition of Quebec as a distinct society.
2)	Guaranteed extended powers over immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank my colleagues for this exception.

Mr. Speaker, I continue.
Third, limit the federal Government's spending power; fourth, review of the Constitution amending formula, including a right of veto for Quebec, and finally, ensure Quebec's participation to the appointment of Supreme Court justices.
In August 1986, in Edmonton, the provincial Premiers unanimously agreed that their first constitutional priority was to consider Quebec's proposals before dealing with any other matter.
I remind the House that a little over a year ago, we had no commitment from the federal Government nor any other indication of its position concerning the constitutional dilemma. I suppose that the federal Government wanted to leave the initiative to others. Such was not the case with us, as members of the Liberal Party, for in the spring of 1986, our Leader (Mr. Turner) clearly defined the constitutional position of the Liberal Party in an interview to the Le Devoir newspaper, and in St-Hyacinthe, in the summer of 1986, he spelled out the whole constitutional amendment in a resolution which was almost unanimously adopted by the Quebec wing of the Liberal Party of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, some wonder why the Liberal Party of Canada supports the Accord, even if we have amendments to propose to improve it. It is quite simple. This Accord resembles as a twin the constitutional resolution adopted in November, 1986, by the Liberal Party during its convention held here in Ottawa.
I should like to describe in general terms the November 1986, resolution adopted by the Liberal Party. It was suggested to add a preamble to the Constitution which would provide for the following a) maintain and reinforce the linguistic duality; b) recognize Quebec's distinct society; c) recognize the
Constitution Amendment, 1987
multicultural nature of Canadian society; d) recognize the contribution of our native peoples; and e) develop Canada as an economic union. Mr. Speaker, such was the resolution adopted by the Ottawa Convention of the Liberal Party in November, 1986.
Moreover, the Liberal Party agreed to carry out a substantial reform of the Senate, while enshrining the principle of double majority in the Senate for all linguistic and cultural legislation. In the area of immigration, it meant to enshrine the Cullen-Couture agreement and to call a federal-provincial conference to deal with the federal government's spending power in the areas of provincial jurisdiction.
Now, this is all included in the Meech Lake Accord and some of my hon. friends opposite do not understand that the position of Liberal party in this regard is consistent and that we will vote for the Meech Lake Constitutional Agreement. Our position is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, and the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) was dead wrong when she said that the Liberals were against it.
We agree with the Meech Lake Accord because it is consistent with our Constitutional resolution of November, 1986. We are introducing amendments to the Meech Lake Accord because our resolution went even further, particularly by amending Section 33 of the Charter, the so-called "notwithstanding" clause-if that clause was deleted, our country would be fairer and safer and the words "where numbers warrant", an assessment of rights, would have to be deleted as well.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party went much further in guaranteeing the protection of minority rights. I have therefore some difficulty with the Accord in particular with regard to the Federal Government's commitment not only to protect but also to promote the equality of status of both official languages.
In fact, one of the main features of the Accord is the recognition in Section 2 of the language duality as a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian society. That Section recognizes Quebec's claim as a distinct society. But in fact, it goes much further because it not only recognizes the distinct identity of Quebec but it is also a recognition of the official language minorities throughout the country and of the fact that those minorities constitute a fundamental characteristic of the Canadian society. Moreover the role of the provinces, outside Quebec, is to preserve that fundamental characteristic of Canada.
If Prime Minister Trudeau had told me at the time, as reported in Hansard of November 9, 1981, in an answer to a question that with the introduction of the Charter of Rights, and I quote: "to start with, it would be good that Francophones outside Quebec rejoice for a little while-", perhaps not for too long, but for a little while, "-because the rights they have have been fighting for for 114 years are at last recognized."

September 29, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Therefore it can be stated, without any reservation that since then, some progress has been made and that the Meech Lake Accord is indeed promoting minority rights. I do rejoice as was suggested by the then Prime Minister. But just for a little while as he also warned me because I would have liked things to move faster. In fact, what Section 2 is doing is to entrench bilingualism in Canada. Yet, bilingualism is a major legacy of former Liberal Governments. As was mentioned in our minority report, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party has always believed in official bilingualism which was first recognized in the Official Languages Act in 1969 and confirmed in the Constitutional Act of 1982. We do not believe that the Langevin Accord might, in any way, jeopardize bilingualism.
Mr. Speaker, our amendment must be considered in the context of the amendment to Section 2 of the Constitution. First it should be said that this is an interpretation clause which applies to the Constitution as a whole. But it is more than just a preamble considering the fact that, from now on, because of its equal status with other interpretation rules, the courts will have to take it into account to interpret the Constitution, including the Charter.
However, it should be mentioned that this clause is not binding and by that I mean that because of the provisions regarding linguistic duality and distinct identity the federal or provincial Governments neither gain or lose any power. This is a mere direction for the courts to get a perspective on the intent of the legislators which is the recognition of official language minorities all across Canada in addition to recognizing the Quebec society as a distinct society.
Concerning the recognition of minorities, the Federation des Francophones hors Quebec would have preferred to see the Accord define language duality and by the same token the existence of minorities by recognizing not only the linguistic identity of an individual as in "French-Speaking Canadian" but also the collective rights of that minority. This change which was made after the Meech Lake Accord appears in the legal text, also called the Langevin Accord where the terms "recognition of French-Speaking Canada", were replaced by "the recognition of French-Speaking Canadians".
The argument put forward by the Federation des Francophones hors Quebec suggested that this wording would make it easier to argue before the courts that the Accord protects collective rights. I fully agree. This wording was rejected mainly because of the potential ambiguity of the recognition given in Section 2. The fact remains that I want to draw the attention of the House to this important aspect because we in the minorities will still depend on a liberal court interpretation of the constitutional text. I sincerely hope we will be entitled to that, although I would have preferred explicit guarantees.
So the linguistic duality is recognized as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. To this fundamental characteristic
we must add, in the case of Quebec, the notion of distinct society. Here again the wording of the legislators leaves ample room for court interpretation as to the exact meaning of the concept of distinct society. In Quebec it includes both anglophones and francophones.
The committee heard every kind of analysis according to the various experts who came to give evidence, but there was no consensus, and that is understandable. But even at that the committee gave their interpretation of the section in light of the notion of linguistic duality as a fundamental characteristic, and they stated in the report:
It is in light of this fundamental characteristic that the courts will be asked to consider Quebec as a distinct society. As it is the proposed amendment does not describe it as a fundamental characteristic.
But this is where things get complicated and, without our proposed amendment, we are again faced with double standards-different treatment for Quebec's anglophone minority.
Indeed, if we analyze the concept of a distinct society for Quebec in the light of linguistic duality, we find in Clause 2.1(3) that the Quebec National Assembly has the role of preserving and promoting the distinct identity of Quebec. But what is this distinct identity, Mr. Speaker? According to the report of the Joint Special Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, on page 33, this phrase indubitably includes the language and the culture of French-speaking Quebecers, but also those of the English-speaking minority.
If we follow this interpretation, a double imbalance is created between the treatment accorded to our minorities, depending on whether they are English-speaking or Frenchspeaking. If the minority is English-speaking, as it is in Quebec, the provincial Government must not only preserve and promote the linguistic duality, but also preserve and promote the particular culture of the anglophone minority.
The Committee goes even further in its interpretation as it includes the native people in the definition of "distinct society". This is what we find in section 40 of the report:
As already pointed out, to the extent that they reside in Quebec, the native people belong to this "distinct society" just as much as the other residents. They have just as much right to benefit from the application of the interpretation rule as concerns the preservation and promotion of the "distinct society". Moreover, the members of the Joint Committee are convinced that other groups could be defined as distinct societies.
Mr. Speaker, I find this enlightening and important. The Accord therefore goes even further as it introduces, in addition to the promotion element which is absent for French-speaking minorities outside Quebec, the element of the particular culture of the minority, as I have already said, which includes not only Quebec francophones, but also the anglophones and the native people. This is potentially a very strong measure for Quebec anglophones and native people. It is up to them to claim their rights in Quebec and demand that their identity be preserved and promoted.
September 29, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I will conclude on that, since I do not want to take too much of the time of the House. The Government, since this debate started, is clamouring far and wide that the Liberal Party wants to amend the Accord, because in their view there is a real need for it. But they also keep repeating that we cannot amend the Accord, because this would be going against Quebec's five conditions. But that is not true, Mr. Speaker. If we had simply respected Quebec's proposals, as stated in August 1986, we would never had committed Quebec to recognizing language rights, either in Quebec or elsewhere. But Quebec went away from Meech Lake ready to bind itself to more than was requested. This means we could have asked and obtained a little bit more, if the Canadian Government had not lacked the political courage and had insisted on selling its wares by telling Quebec: You must recognize also that it is our responsibility as the federal Government not only to protect but to to promote language duality.
Mr. Speaker, the way this Government is going about it in the free-trade negotiations with the Americans, the question that arises is how the constitutional negotiations were conducted. The Government told us that any change would mean the end of the Accord because the English-speaking provinces did not want to grant anything more to their minorities.
Mr. Speaker, in my view that is not the spirit that prevails in my country. However, we were able to ask them for a constitutional recognition, an extra obligation, and this is why I support that amended constitution, because we gained something. We now have a clear and specific definition of this country which says that the provinces and the Canadian Government must safeguard the existence of both language groups in this country, the English-speaking in Quebec and the French-speaking outside Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to go somewhat further and ask the Canadian Government to assume its responsibilities and actually take over the situation of French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec and generously accept the amendment we are proposing, namely that the Canadian Government should bind itself to promoting the English and French reality in Canada- throughout Canada-and to do so immediately.

speechtext:
that Bill C-260, an Act respecting Sir John A. Macdonald Day, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am honoured and obviously very pleased to introduce Bill C-260, an Act respecting Sir John A. Macdonald Day. If Hon. Members agree with and see fit to support this measure, it would create for the first time a national holiday in February to honour Canada's first Prime Minister.
This idea has been discussed by various individuals throughout the years. In fact, there is an organized movement in Kingston, Ontario, the city in which I had the pleasure to attend Queen's University a few years ago. The City of Kingston holds celebrations in February of each year to honour its most famous citizen. I think it is fitting that the movement for a holiday began there. Now I believe it is appropriate that the holiday be extended by Parliament to the entire nation.
Sir John A. Macdonald was born in Glasgow in 1815 of Scottish parents. His grandfather fought for Prince Charles Edward Stuart at the Battle of Culloden Moor in 1745. When Sir John A. was five, his family moved from Scotland and settled in the Kingston area in the year 1820.
Like so many other great politicians, Sir John A. Macdonald became a lawyer and was admitted to the Bar in 1836. In 1844, he continued his political career with his election as the Conservative Member for Kingston in the Legislative Assembly of the Province of Canada. He became joint premier of a Liberal-Conservative coalition in 1858 and it was in subsequent years while he held that position that Sir John A. began his lifelong quest as a result of his deep belief that there should be a federation of all British North American colonies. As a result, he was a moving force in the Charlottetown and Quebec conferences of 1864 and acted as chairman of the London conference in December of 1866 at which he used his great constitutional expertise, knowledge and ability to put the finishing touches on the British North America Act of 1867, the Act which created the Dominion of Canada on July 1, 1867.
If Sir John A. did nothing else after that time, I believe his place in Canadian history would be secure and he would be worthy of our honour. However, as we all know, he did much more than that. I think all Canadians recognize his importance in the subsequent years until his death in 1891 and the contributions he made to Canada.

September 29, 1987
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
Sir John A. Macdonald recognized very early on the importance of territorial expansion to secure this country's independence on this half of the continent. Under his prime ministership, we saw the expansion of the country to Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island. We saw the completion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the railway which was so vital in securing Canada's unity over the years.
I propose that a national holiday be declared in this man's honour. There will be those who will ask me at what cost we will have another national holiday. It is my understanding that in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Australia and a whole host of other western industrialized countries, the people celebrate more national holidays than Canadians. I suggest that it has not been to their detriment to celebrate those national holidays, just as I believe it will not be to the detriment and indeed would be to the benefit of Canada.
I suggest that it is impossible to calculate the benefits of a new national holiday in February. All of us have heard stories of the depression suffered by many Canadians during that time of the year. In that stretch between New Year's and Easter, there are presently no holidays. I suggest that there would be a tremendous increase in employee morale and I would suggest, as others have, that there would be a decrease in absenteeism if there were to be a holiday in February. As well, I would suggest that Canadians are now trying to do everything possible to extend our tourist season into the winter months. I believe it would be of tremendous benefit to the tourist industry to have a long weekend in February.
As well, such a holiday would focus attention on a vital chapter in Canada's history. Anyone who has grown up in Canada will have heard it said time and time again that we Canadians do not spend enough time examining our history and celebrating the individuals who helped build Canada. Indeed, as a student at Valleyway Public School, I recall hearing a succession of teachers raise the subject of Sir John A. Macdonald and telling us of his importance to the creation of Canada. I recall that each of them made the comment that perhaps someday Canada will have a holiday to honour this great man. I suggest that the talk you have heard so often from Canadians about promoting our history will remain just that unless we do some of the concrete things necessary to have the opportunity to examine and celebrate our history. I suggest that this Chamber has an opportunity this afternoon to do something very constructive to promote one of the great figures in Canadian history.
One of my colleagues said to me that there are certain partisan considerations in this. This may not go through by reason of the fact that Sir. John A. Macdonald was a Conservative. I should say that, among other things, it is perhaps not well-known that Sir John A. Macdonald was a participant in a number of coalitions. I mentioned already that he was Prime Minister under a Liberal-Conservative coalition.
However, regarding the partisan issue, I remember this House taking time to pass a resolution with the support of all three Parties to erect a statue on Parliament Hill to Lester B. Pearson. Before I became a Member of Parliament the Department of External Affairs building in Ottawa was named after Mr. Pearson, as was the Toronto International Airport. I believe there is a university in British Columbia named after him as well. That is all well and good. All Canadians, regardless of their political affiliation, agree with that. I was in this Chamber over two years when a resolution was put forward to erect a statue on Parliament Hill to John Diefenbaker. I participated in the debate and saw this Chamber rise above partisan considerations to honour a man who was perhaps one of the most partisan politicians in Canadian history. I remember as well the day when Tommy Douglas died and this Chamber took the time to remember him. I remember the heartfelt comments out of the mouths of politicians of all political Parties in recognizing his achievements as Premier of Saskatchewan, Leader of the CCF, and first Leader of the NDP. I agreed with those because I think they were appropriate.
Although this Chamber is a very partisan place on a day-today basis, we have seen three examples where we have risen above that. I suggest to Members of this House that this is another one of those opportunities to pay homage to a man whose contributions to this country are recognized by everyone. As an example of that, on his passing in 1891 Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke about Sir John A. Macdonald on behalf of his Party. All his comments were very interesting, but I will bring only a couple of them to the attention of this House in order to demonstrate the point I am trying to make. He said this:
It may be said without any exaggeration whatever, that the life of Sir John A. Macdonald, from the date he entered Parliament is the history of Canada-
Later on he said:
Today, we deplore the loss of him who, we all unite in saying, was the foremost Canadian of his time, and who filled the largest place in Canadian history.
I find it significant that I am asking Parliament to honour a man who did so much to build and unite Canada on the very same day that we commenced debate on a great constitutional agreement which I believe all Members believe to be constructive in our efforts towards uniting Canada. I believe that most people in Canada will applaud the action we might take here this afternoon.
I would like to conclude with words that Sir John A. Macdonald wrote just shortly before his death and which I believe sum up his goals for this country. He said:
If I had influence over the minds of the people of Canada, any power over their intellect, I would leave them with the legacy:
Whatever you do adhere to the union-we are a great country, and shall become one of the greatest in the universe if we preserve it; we shall sink into insignificance and adversity if we suffer it to be broken. God and nature have made the two Canadas one-let no factious men be allowed to put them asunder.

Hear, hear!
September 29, 1987

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOLIDAYS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish there were more than 10 minutes available to me to dedicate to this subject. It deserves a great deal more time than that. As well, I would like to add my admonition to that of my friend who introduced the Bill in saying this should not be a partisan debate if at all possible. This subject deserves the consideration of all political Parties and all Members of Parliament, especially those who are proud of Canada.
We all know that when Sir John A. Macdonald entered politics in 1844 the nation that was to become Canada was simply a string of colonies spread out from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. When he ended his political career there was a nation literally from sea to sea. It was Sir John A. Macdonald who had the vision and the courage to carry it forward. We all know that, if it had not been for his leadership and inspiration, this Canada might not exist today. Indeed, we certainly know that he, with his understanding and determination, was largely responsible for bringing about Confederation. We know it was he who arranged for the purchase of the entire Northwest Territories from the Hudson Bay Company and saw to it that that vast stretch of territory was added to this nation. It was Sir John A. Macdonald who built the railroad from sea to sea. In other words, in this man's achievements we see almost everything that constitutes nation-building and the establishment of this nation.
It is therefore regrettable that we do not have any special recognition of that man and what he has done for this country. Indeed, when he died he was buried in a cemetery in Catara-qui, near Kingston. Interestingly enough, even today there is no special sign or marking to direct people to the grave. The place where he lies buried is relatively unknown to most Canadians.
On October 5, 1979, I introduced a Private Members' Bill entitled "An Act to Proclaim a Day in Commemoration of Sir John A. Macdonald". Again in 1981, about a year and a half later, I introduced a motion under Standing Order 43 calling for recognition of Sir John A. Macdonald and a day to be declared in his honour. As a matter of fact, the motion was seconded by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), which I felt was appropriate. Unfortunately, that resolution was not carried unanimously.
I said earlier that I would not like this to be a partisan speech. However, regrettably, there was a gaggle of "noes" to that resolution, and it did not come from the benches of either the Liberal or the Conservative Parties.
I am happy that the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) has indicated his support for such a day. I hope that Members of all Parties will rise above all partisan considerations and give sympathetic consideration to this Bill.
I realize that there are problems involved in proclaiming a national holiday because that would mean another day off work. That might concern businessmen, and I can certainly
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
understand their concerns. That is why when I introduced my Bill and my motion I called for a day to memorialize him, not necessarily with a day off work.
I personally think there is a good argument for a day off work. I think that the suggestion made by my colleague is a good one. A holiday in February is much needed in this country. I think that every effort should be made at least to study his suggestion. I hope his suggestion will be approved by this House in Private Members' Hour, that it will go to committee where further study can be given to it and, if appropriate, amendments made. The Government could even make it its own Bill if that is necessary. I do hope it will receive the support of all Members.
I want to conclude my remarks with a tribute to another man who has been working very hard for many years on this project. His name is Harvey Haber. In fact, an editorial in The Toronto Star was dedicated to him and his work on January 11, 1982, when The Toronto Star came out in favour of a John A. Macdonald Day on that date.
Harvey Haber has pointed out, as he has worked year after year to try to achieve support for recognition of this day, that school children in this country can tell you who was the first President of the United States but often cannot tell you who was the first Prime Minister of Canada. If you ask them whether they have ever heard of the name Macdonald, they will say "Yes, Ronald McDonald".
I hope that through the action of the House of Commons that tragedy will come to an end, that through our action Canadian school children will become more knowledgeable about the history of this great country and of the man who did so much to establish it. I hope that when they hear the name Macdonald they will chime, "Yes, Sir John A. Macdonald".

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOLIDAYS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to indicate my support and that of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party for this proposal. It is not surprising that someone who represents an area like Winnipeg, with the kind of weather we get there in February, would support a suggestion that we have a holiday in February. As has already been pointed out, there is no holiday between New Year's and Easter.
There have been a number of attempts to get Parliament to approve a proposal that we set aside a day to honour Sir John A. Macdonald. There have been a number of proposals made by some of my former colleagues that we set aside a day to be named Heritage Day. In doing that we would be following the example of some other countries such as the United States which has designated both Lincoln's birthday and Washington's birthday as national holidays. For many years we in this country designated May 24, the birth date of Queen Victoria, as a holiday.
I want to talk about Sir John A. Macdonald. The fact is that he was not just one of the Fathers of Confederation. It is likely that without Sir John A. Macdonald the country of Canada

September 29, 1987
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
would not exist. In looking at the map of North America it is very easy to see that the economic lines in North America really run north and south rather than east and west. It was Sir John A. MacDonald's determination that the northern half of North America not become part of the United States which drove him to make two important principles a fundamental part of his political philosophy. Without those two principles Canada would probably not exist.
The first, of course, was his understanding that without a railway which spanned the continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific Canada could not become a country. The second principle to which he ascribed and which he made a fundamental part of his policy was the national policy. That was traditional Tory policy, similar in Canada to the Tory policy in Great Britain. That was a policy of protectionism for Canadian industry and manufacturing. Sir John A. Macdonald saw that without that we would not be able to keep this disparate nation together.
For the first time we saw assertiveness by Canada on economic matters. We started a manufacturing industry which substituted Canadian-made goods for what was previously imported from the mother country, Great Britain, or from the United States. It was a policy which worked for Canada and for Sir John A. Macdonald.
While I endorse this resolution, I must ask myself what has happened to the political Parties in this country. Sir John A. Macdonald instituted the first protectionist policy, the first tariff system in this country, and he was the Leader of the Conservative Party. He was opposed by the Liberals under Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
We should all remember that election campaign when Sir Wilfrid Laurier, speaking for his Liberal Party, proposed reciprocity with the United States. The Conservative Party opposed that. Now in 1987 we have had a complete reversal. The Conservatives, the inheritors of the tradition and the ideas of Sir John A. Macdonald, are hell-bent for election to get a free trade agreement with the United States. It does not matter what the cost is or what we have to give up, they will do it. The Liberal Party, which under Sir Wilfrid Laurier was all for free trade, is finally realizing that free trade with the United States would create many problems.
Let us make no mistake, Macdonald found that his carefully founded national policy was a success. I will quote a few sentences from the most Tory of Canadian historians, Donald Creighton, who in his two-volume biography of Sir John A. Macdonald said at page 275 the following:
And yet, as the long, warm, golden autumn of 1879 drew placidly on, he began at last to concede, even to himself, that the improvement was a miraculous certainty.
Everything showed it. The harvest had been bountiful. Prices were going up. The volume of imports slowly declined, while that of exports began to rise steadily upwards. "Trade is recovering wonderfully . . . Lome wrote proudly to Hicks Beach. The ministers gloated. And Macdonald knew that the whole future of his government had been dramatically changed. Within a year of his accession to office, his commercial programme had been vindicated by a
demonstration as convincing as it was fortuitous. The national policy was borne away towards success on the swift wheels of an accelerating prosperity. For a time, while this good fortune lasted, he would be able to do almost anything successfully. He might even succeed-it would be the supreme piece of luck-in inducing a commercial company to take over the whole gigantic project of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Obviously my friends in the Conservative Party, if they ever knew anything about the history of Canada, have forgotten it all. I would suggest quite seriously to the Prime Minister that he take a little time to read Donald Creighton's biography of Sir John A. Macdonald. If he did, he would not be so hell-bent to get this free trade deal. It was an idea he rejected vehemently before he became the Prime Minister. He would begin to think about what is good for Canada, as did Sir John A. Macdonald. If he did, this would be a better country.
Let me conclude by saying again that I and my colleagues in the New Democratic Party will be very happy to support the proposal we are discussing today.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOLIDAYS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues I am very pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-260 introduced by my colleague from Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) to designate the second Monday of February as Sir John A. Macdonald Day.
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks I should like to make a brief comment and say I found it rather deplorable that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) was unable to do as the Hon. Member for Eglington-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) did, as he said, and refrain from taking a partisan approach to such an interesting debate. He concluded by saying that he agrees, that he is in favour of the motion, but throughout his remarks he did manage to criticize Sir John A. Macdonald or the Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, Sir John A. Macdonald presided over the birth of Canada as a nation. His administration was witness to Canada's tremendous expansion, from coast to coast, from south to north, as far as the Arctic islands. I am sure all Canadians share the commendable sentiment expressed through the motion before us today. Many things could be said concerning this proposed legal holiday in his honour. For openers, notwithstanding the wishes of many people to have a new legal holiday, we must not forget that we already have July 1, Canada Day, a great holiday for all Canadians. Every year, Mr. Speaker, this holiday gives us an opportunity to honour all our Prime Ministers and, I might add, all Canadian men and women who, before or after Confederation, contributed to the growth, diversity and strength of this remarkable country in which we Canadians live.
Since the name of Sir John A. Macdonald is mentioned on every such occasion, I wonder whether it is necessary indeed to have a distinct legal holiday. There is not doubt that the motion is highly commendable.
September 29, 1987

Yet, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that before setting up a new holiday, it would be better to reconsider its name. For I think that the basic idea is to pay tribute to our Founding Fathers. We should take this opportunity to think of a name which would include all the individuals who, through their efforts and determination, managed to create a wonderful nation, the Canada of 1867.
The names of other people should be included, such as Sir George Etienne Cartier, who worked very closely with Sir John A. Macdonald both before and after Confederation and whose office in the East Block on the Hill is recognized as an historical site, just as the office of Sir John A. Macdonald, which is close by, is recognized as an historical site.
If we think of other great Canadians who came from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or other provinces, the name of Joe Smallwood, who was responsible for Newfoundland and Labrador joining Confederation in 1949, comes to mind. Nearer to us, if we think of the new Constitutional Accord, this historical document which was signed in June in Lange-vin-Meech, we could include without hesitation the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I am sure that, with the exception of a few ill-intentioned Liberals and our Socialists who are constantly hiding behind a screen of hypocrisy, most Canadians would agree that the name of this Prime Minister should be included.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, instead of choosing only one name for this holiday, we should try to come up with a name which would be more "generic" and which would be an opportunity to pay tribute to a great many Canadian men and women for their contributions.
Another point not to be overlooked is that of the cost of such a holiday. A paid holiday would represent a major expense for employers in the form of employee benefits. I have been advised that for the federal Government alone, including Public Service employees, the members of the Armed Forces, the RCMP, etc., one more holiday would cost over $50 million.
Mr. Speaker, although this motion is praiseworthy and means to pay tribute to a great Prime Minister and a great Canadian, I think it would be important for the government to pay more attention to the objectives and the costs of such a holiday and to be able to consider other options for a holiday in February, an idea which all Canadians would applaud.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on this important Bill put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson). Sir John A. Macdonald was a remarkable man. It is only fitting that we remember him in many ways.
I would like to talk about some of his achievements and that important place from which he comes, Kingston. It was mentioned by my hon. friend from Niagara Falls that he attended Queens University. Queens is a university close to my
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
heart. I have two children who graduated from that university. I suppose that points out the difference in our generations.
As we all know, Sir John A. Macdonald formed the Dominion of Canada by uniting the four provinces. To those four provinces he added the west. He took a huge country and fought a great many people who did not have much vision. Sir John A. Macdonald was a man with a great deal of vision. With that vision he was able to convince those of lesser vision of the importance of having a strong central Canada made up of the provinces he had welded together. He had a great deal of conviction, as we all know, which enabled him and others to put our Confederation together. He brought our country together as a result of the drive which he had to create a national railroad.
We must talk and think about this great Prime Minister, this great father of our country, in many ways and at all times. With respect to establishing holidays, with all due respect, I become somewhat concerned sometimes about the number of holidays that we already have. I have a great deal of work to do in my job, and I would have a problem completing it if we had more holidays. I do not know what I would do if there were more holidays. I ask Hon. Members to look at all the work that is piled up here on my desk.
There are concerns which the federal Government has in terms of establishing another holiday. One of the concerns is with respect to whether or not that would place some sort of pressure on the provinces to follow suit. Then there are the costs to consider.
In talking about holidays, I was in another country recently and it seemed as though there was a holiday there every other day. Productivity falls off when there are too many holidays. I think there are a great many concerns in that respect.
Recognizing Sir John A. Macdonald by commemorating a statutory holiday in his name would be great. I do not know if all here assembled know that the former Prime Minister Alexander Mackenzie is from Sarnia. We do not have a national holiday in his name. I have somewhat of a problem supporting the commemoration of a holiday in the name of one Prime Minister when there is not one for Alexander Mackenzie.
Mr. Red way: He also represented York East at one time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I want to commend my colleague, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson) for his proposal to pay tribute to the man who presided over the building of Canada as we know it, who presided over the recognition of one Canada from sea to sea, and right up to the Arctic Ocean. It is therefore important that we pay him a tribute that is significant. Since I referred to the Arctic Ocean, I would also take this opportunity to pay tribute to someone in my constituency who brought the Arctic lands under Canada's flag-the first Arctic explorer, Captain Bernier, a native of my constituency whose remains rest in my constituency.
John A. Macdonald's main work, excluding Canada's official foundation, was to make this country a reality not only in the geographic sense, but to have it made a reality through union with rails. During the 25 years that Mr. Macdonald was Prime Minister of Canada, tremendous difficulties were also overcome to forge the link that was needed at that point and that is still very important, the link that united Canada from East to West, with the aim at that time to protect it against integration into the United States.
The year 1986 indeed marked the 100th anniversary of this rail link which is approximately 3,200 miles long. Celebrations were held in June, 1986. Strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, this material union of Canada took place under a Conservative Government, and today, one century later, we Conservatives are again the ones to develop and improve this union, and we now want to provide Canadians with a North-South link. This is why the Conservative Government is trying to ensure a market in the United States for this generation and the ones that will follow. One hundred years ago, we forged our East-West links under a Conservative Government, and today, still under a Conservative Government, we are trying to establish a North-South link to integrate our own economy to the American economy and provide for all our producers an additional market of 250 million potential customers. It is also a good thing to pay tribute to a former Prime minister of Canada and to a French-speaking Canadian who supported him from the very beginning, Sir George-Etienne Cartier, who should also be mentioned when we pay hommage to those who built Canada.
However, in a capitalistic system, something that we must keep in mind is the cost of institutionalizing a holiday, and I believe that Mr. Macdonald himself would object to our making our production even more expensive, especially as concerns our exports to the United States and to the rest of the world. With a gross national product of $500 billion, one day
off work means a loss of $2.5 billion in production, Mr. Speaker.
I therefore believe that we should respect the spirit of Mr. Macdonald, who would not want us to spend this much money if he were still here.

Since we have many new Pages who come from all across Canada, I felt that I should indicate that, of course, anything to honour our Canadian Fathers should be considered by the House. If we wish to build and create a country-I always claim that Canada is one of the few countries in the world that is making itself every day. That is bad English, but I do wish to communicate my sentiments in English concerning Sir John A. Macdonald.
Canada is a country in the making every day. When speaking of February, it reminds me of another great event which took place on February 15, 1965. To educate our young university people, February 15 was the official day when we
September 29, 1987

raised our Canadian flag. 1 did respect, and I still respect today those who saw another flag going to the Archives of Canada and being replaced by a truly Canadian flag. The Bill of our esteemed colleague reminds me that there has been much talk about that type of celebration in February.
I remember a very esteemed colleague from the Conservative Party, then in the Opposition, who wished to make the second Monday of February Fleritage Day to honour Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir George-Etienne Cartier, and all the Fathers of Confederation, plus the flag of Canada.
In my evaluation, it is good that from time to time we spend an hour to remind ourselves of the manner in which this country came about, especially now that we are debating the very important issue called the Meech Lake agreement. I prefer to call it the Langevin accord, because Meech Lake has been amended by the Langevin accord. In my humble evaluation, everybody is erroneously calling it the Meech Lake agreement while we should more justly say the Langevin accord. There was an amendment that Premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) made to the Meech Lake Accord during this great event that took place at the Langevin Building.
However, as I said, I believe the House should consider honouring Sir John A. Macdonald. Should it be a holiday? Why not? Everyone likes a holiday. I do not know of any Canadian who would not like a holiday in February.

speechtext: Especially in February.

speechtext:
"Especially in February", as my esteemed colleague Stan Darling says. I hope that during Private Members' Hour we can call each other by name and not by constituency. As my esteemed friend, who has been a longtime member of the Standing Committee on National Defence and is from Parry Sound-Muskoka, is saying, anything in February would be good.
Seriously, however, there are many other events which we should celebrate. Perhaps some day we could combine them and do it during February. I am very serious; I do not want to be accused of wandering from the Bill which is being debated. If we want to honour Sir John A. Macdonald in a very relaxed atmosphere, we must ask ourselves what it would represent.
It would represent the beginning of what was then known as Canada. If such a thing were to take place, perhaps we could call it Confederation Day, but we do have July 1 for that purpose. Perhaps it could be the Fathers of Confederation or the National Anthem. It was in 1965, 1966, and 1967 that a committee of the House of Commons-and the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and I are the only two remaining members of that committee-recommended "O Canada" as the National Anthem. It took approximately 15 years before we proclaimed it. It only became official on July 1, 1980, even though some Canadians had been singing it
Sir John A. Macdonald Day
since July 1, 1880 when Calixa Lavallee and Judge Adolphe-Basile Routhier got together and wrote the words and music for "O Canada". That shows how slow we can sometimes be in terms of Canadianization. It was in 1980 that we proclaimed it as the official National Anthem. Some people say that perhaps sometime in February we should celebrate National Anthem Day.
Why should we honour the national flag, the National Anthem, or Sir John A. Macdonald? It is because there are so many millions of new Canadians who should be sensitized to what Canada is all about. Hon. Members will know that I wanted to honour John Diefenbaker by having his image on a Canadian coin. Some people thought it was a direct attack on the monarchy. I had no such sentiments. Canadians, especially new ones, should know what Canada is all about. When they have money in their hands every day, for example a five-dollar bill, eventually they say: "Who is that guy?" To the best of my recollection it would be the image of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the five dollar bill, the image of Sir John A. Macdonald on the ten-dollar bill, and the image of Mackenzie King on the fifty-dollar bill. It is a very indirect way to educate ourselves on what Canada is all about.
I was very pleased and honoured to put forward a proposal to honour John Diefenbaker by placing his image on a Canadian coin. Later we could honour Lester B. Pearson and Louis St. Laurent. Of course we cannot honour people who are still alive; they may use that to come back. Who knows?
If I were asked to vote today, I would be very happy to honour Sir John A. Macdonald. I would go along with it. However, along with that, we should also honour all the others who have done so much. I think that would be great for us, for the new young Pages working in the House of Commons, and for millions of people who recently came to Canada. We must be reminded of what Canada is all about, and a Bill of that kind should do it.

We should congratulate the Hon. Member because as a result of such an initiative, our institutions get to be more widely known. Thus we learn about the early days of our country and what should be revered. In spite of everything, Canada is a country which has weathered many storms and will continue to do. I thank you for your forbearance, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN RELATIONS WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN RELATIONS WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 know that you, and I know for certain that I, very strongly, very vehemently and very unswervingly oppose apartheid. I know that you and I as well find apartheid to be institutionalized racism. We find it reprehensible and we support policies to encourage a peaceful solution and a peaceful end to apartheid in South Africa. Those are positions with which virtually all Canadians agree. However, all Canadians do not agree on what policies we should be following in order to bring about an end to apartheid.
The national polls tell us that a clear majority of Canadians agree with the policies the present Government is following. Those policies include increased sanctions, an anti-apartheid register, an embargo on arms and spare parts sales, a code of conduct for employment practices for Canadian corporations and businesses carrying on business in South Africa and financial assistance to South African blacks through education and training. As well, efforts are being made to get other nations through the Commonwealth, the francophonie and other western industrialized groups to support efforts against apartheid. Of course, there has been a continuing dialogue
between Canada and South Africa with respect to bringing to a peaceful end the policies of apartheid.
Others are saying, however, that they do not agree with those policies. 1 am sure that you get those messages just as I do, Mr. Speaker. I receive many calls and letters from people in my constituency who feel very strongly that the approach that is being taken is the wrong one. It is not because they agree with apartheid or feel it is a good policy to be followed. They feel the approach being taken will perhaps encourage violence and terrorism and Marxism and communism, and bring about the establishment of a Soviet form of Government in South Africa. They do not want to see that. I know you do not want to see that, and I do not want to see it either.
Interestingly enough, I ran a survey in my constituency about a year ago on this question. I asked the following: Do you think Canada should impose economic sanctions against South Africa? Do you think we should increase economic sanctions? Some 37.8 per cent said yes and 52.6 per cent said no. I asked: Do you think we should have total sanctions against South Africa? I had 29.3 per cent say yes and 59.7 per cent say no. That is in a constituency where 51 per cent of the residents come from neither anglophone nor francophone background. There are over 60 different cultural and ethnic backgrounds represented in that constituency. This is a very interesting result in a part of the country such as mine.
As I indicated, I think the crux of the problem lies with the concern about whether or not the policies being followed by the Government are in effect encouraging establishment of a communist form of Government in southern Africa. On the other hand, there are those who say we must follow the policies this Government is following now. One of those persons is the Reverend Johannes Sindano. He is a Lutheran evangelical pastor and I had the opportunity of meeting him here in Ottawa. He comes from southern Africa and he put it to me and others that met with him that it is important for Canada and other western nations to put pressure on the South African Government to bring about an end to apartheid. To remain silent will be to create just the opposite of the desired effect. If the West does not encourage black South Africans, they will turn to the eastern bloc for encouragement and support in their struggle against apartheid. After all, as he points out, because black Africans are in the majority it is inevitable at some point in time that apartheid will disappear. At that stage they will remember who their friends and supporters were, whether they be in the eastern bloc or in western nations.
He also pointed out that, naturally, black Africans look to the West for support and help. He said it is from the West that black Africans received their education. It is from the West they received their religious training, economic development, and the higher standard of living that many of them now enjoy. It is natural for black South Africans to look to the West rather than the East. After all, it was Jefferson, not Lenin, who said all men were created equal. It was Lincoln
September 29, 1987

who took the chains of slavery off blacks in America, and Stalin who enslaved eastern Europe.
Again, it is natural for black Africa to look to the West for support. Again, if the support is not forthcoming, unfortunately the vacuum will be filled, as the Reverend Sindano pointed out to me, by the eastern bloc. That may also bring about the violence which Canadians certainly do not want, notwithstanding the comments of our colleagues in the House, the NDP, who, a week or two ago, indicated that they felt violence was justifiable. I do not think the vast majority of Canadians feel that way. They want a peaceful solution in South Africa.
The Government has heard all sides of the story. It has heard the people who say that we must support South African blacks through more pressure. It has heard those who believe that we should keep our hands off South Africa. It is now up to the Government to respond and tell us what it is going to do in this situation.
I am looking forward to hearing from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight whether the Government is wavering in its stance on South Africa or whether it will maintain the strong policy which it has put in place and keep pressure on the South African Government to bring an end to apartheid.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN RELATIONS WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) met with African National Congress President Oliver Tambo one month ago in Ottawa. The Secretary of State for External Affairs had previously held meetings with senior representatives of the ANC, most recently during his trip to South Africa last month.
These meetings do not convey any form of official recognition of the ANC on the part of the Canadian Government. The Government does recognize, however, that the ANC is an important factor in South Africa. It will be part of the solution in that country, whenever it comes and however it comes. There are also other groups with a part to play in building a post-apartheid South Africa.
The Government's objective is to encourage a peaceful solution in South Africa which results in non-racial representative government. Peace and democracy in South Africa are more likely to be achieved by dealing with the ANC and encouraging it to follow a moderate path.
In their meetings with Mr. Tambo, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs explored the prospects for dialogue between the South African Government and the ANC. Mr. Tambo was encouraged to pursue the path of dialogue as was the South Africa Foreign Minister when the Minister met him in August.
The Government of Canada does not condone violence by any of the parties in South Africa, whether by the state or the ANC. The Prime Minister was very clear on that question
Adjournment Debate
during his visit to South Africa in January and that position has been reiterated on a number of other occasions, including directly to Mr. Tambo. Nevertheless, the Government recognizes that the root of violence in South Africa is the racially based system of apartheid and that such an oppressive system, when peaceful means are closed, gives rise to violent opposition.
The ANC had a history of 50 years of non-violence before it was banned. Its present leadership includes many who are moderate and they are to be encouraged. The danger exists, however, that as the level of violence in South Africa continues to grow, so may the influence of more radical elements of the ANC.
To achieve the goal of a peaceful solution to the situation in South Africa Canada has worked successfully with others in the Commonwealth and elsewhere to put pressure on the South African Government to enter into a dialogue with authentic black leaders, including the ANC, and start the process of fundamental change.
PENITENTIARIES-PROVISION OF HEALTH CARE SERVICES/ GOVERNMENT POLICY

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I asked a question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) with regard to the proposed privatization of the health care section of the correctional services. I was not surprised that the Minister's answer was not relevant to my question since the Minister of Justice is not responsible for the correctional system.
My question arose out of a letter which I received from the President of the Professional Institute of the Public Service which I believe exposes a very serious situation regarding the provision of services in our penitentiaries. We must realize that the inmates of our penitentiaries have been involved in very serious crimes; rape, armed robbery and murder. You name it and some of the prisoners have been involved in it.
The Government wishes to extend its policy of privatization wherever possible into the federal penitentiaries. I call that policy objective bizarre for the reason I have already indicated. We are dealing with very angry and disturbed people. It is not surprising that the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada Opposed this idea. The union represents these people. There were 1,440 nurses and psychologists and others who signed a petition against this idea of privatization. One would think that the Department and the Government would have at least talked to these people before they proposed such an unworkable idea.
Second, the Professional Institute in a letter written to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher), signed by the President of the Professional Institute, Iris Craig, makes the following point which I think is very important:

September 29, 1987
Adjournment Debate
CSC claims it wants to save taxpayers' money by laying off its own qualified, well-trained staff and hire contract employees who are simply not equipped to deal with volatile situations in which security is of prime concern.
To work competently in a correctional setting requires a repeated, consistent exposure to that environment. An incorrect decision, or even a lack of a decision, when confronted with a dangerous or life-threatening situation, can escalate into tragedy. There is no substitute for experience.
Surely even this Government should recognize the kind of riots and disturbances going on in our correctional institutions and how important it is to have well-trained, competent, permanent employees who have experience.
I would like to relate an experience my daughter had. She is a new graduate social worker. She received a contract with the John Howard Society. Her job was to work with prisoners in the medium security section of the Stony Mountain penitentiary. One of her clients, as she saw him week after week, was becoming increasingly disturbed, so much so that the last time she saw him she stood with her hand on the handle of the door so that she could get out of the room quickly if necessary. She reported the matter to the prison psychiatrist. He could not or would not do anything about it. A week or two later, while driving her car, she heard a news flash on the radio that a prisoner, her client, had picked up a piece of two-by-four in the carpentry shop, hit the instructor over the head and killed him.
That is the kind of situation which occurs, and this Government is proposing to turn over that work to part-time people on contract whose only interest will be to earn some money, a contractor interested in making a profit.
There are all sorts of questions which must be asked. Who is going to be responsible in a situation like that? Who would the family sue? Would the family sue the Government or would they sue the private contractor? What would be the level of profitability? What rate of return would be considered correct? Once the private sector becomes established will it skim off the profitable and low-risk offenders, leaving the public system with a difficult and unmanageable problem? Will the monitoring and contract requirements ensure business motives do not override the objective rehabilitation and decent prison conditions?
Lastly, I point out to the Parliamentary Secretary who will be answering my questions that a study was done by the Government for the Solicitor General in 1985. It was entitled "Operational and Resource Management, Review 7, Privatization" and warned that privatization could lead to endanger-ment to public, staff and inmates, deterioration of inmates' rights and labour unrest. Clearly, none of us wants this, and that is the burden of my question and my intervention in the House today. I hope the Government can supply some answers today and rethink what I consider to be a totally improper and unworkable idea. It could not be done in a worse set of circumstances than in the correctional system.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: APARTHEID-SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN RELATIONS WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this
opportunity to speak further to the issue raised on September 25, 1987, by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), that being the presumption that the correctional service will be proceeding to the wholesale privatization of health care in its penitentiaries.
First, let me put to rest the myth that privatization of health services involves the replacement of professionals by "poorly-trained part-time workers", as the Hon. Member puts it. Privatization is not a new concept in the health care field. Approximately 40 per cent of the correctional service's health care budget is now spent on professional service contracts with individual professionals such as physicians, psychiatrists, psychologists, and dentists, throughout Canada's penitentiary system. This has been the case for several years. Neither quality of service nor the security of penitentiaries has been compromised by the engagement of such professionals under contract. There is no reason to believe that further privatization in the area of nursing services would lead to such a situation.
I believe that the concern expressed by the Hon. Member may be traced to a review of health care services that has been conducted recently in the Ontario Region of the Correctional Service under the "make or buy policy" of the Treasury Board. Basically, the application of this policy involves a comparison of the costs of providing service "in-house", so to speak, by government employees against the cost of delivery of the same services by the private sector.
This review, which has not yet been completed, is but one part of a major review of the entire field of health care delivery in the correctional service in order to ensure that the level of care provided to inmates takes into account both their specific needs and the level of care offered to society as a whole, and that the means of delivery remains as efficient and effective as possible.
I must emphasize that the only institutions at which nursing services have been privatized are at the new Donnacona Institution in Quebec and Atlantic Institution in New Brunswick. There are no plans at this time to privatize such services further.
The study cited above is restricted to the Ontario Region. Both the Professional Institution of the Public Service and staff in Ontario penitentiaries have been briefed on the objectives of the study. In addition, and most significantly, assurances have been given that employees would not suffer loss of employment if privatization is pursued.
Finally, having emphasized that no further plans for privatization of health services have been formulated, I believe it is also vital that I mention that on any given working day private individuals from the community enter our penitentiaries to provide a wide range of services from dentistry to volunteer literacy training. The qualifications of those persons to enter and provide services is a matter of scrutiny by the correctional service and measures continue to be applied

equally to ensure the safety of their persons and the security of the institution at all times.
POLICIES TOWARD UNITED STATES/GOVERNMENT POSITION

Mr. Speaker, at this stage following a question I asked in the House of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) some months ago, it is clear that the acid rain policy of the Government is in a shambles.
In 1985 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) lost a valuable year by agreeing that the two acid rain envoys prepare a report. In 1986, the same Prime Minister gave the wrong signal to Washington and to the Americans by agreeing to a five-year program on clean coal technology. This indicated to the Americans an implicit willingness on our part to wait for five years. In April of this year in this Chamber the Prime Minister claimed victory when President Reagan made a commitment to consider an acid rain treaty with Canada.
Today, six months later, what do we see on the horizon? It is in this respect that I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will answer. Having claimed victory so many times the credibility of the Prime Minister is now running very thin.
At the same time, it is this Government that has abandoned Canada's role internationally. This is a role which Canada conducted quite successfully until it was abandoned in 1985 by this Government. That international role was intended to generate pressure on the U.S. to come to the table and to agree to a reduction in air pollution through our friends and allies, through those who have adhered to the Helsinki Protocol. Yet unfortunately that initiative was abandoned.
In recent weeks the Americans have accused Canada of not implementing a domestic program to cut acid rain pollution in Canada. The two Tory Provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are the only provinces which still have to come on board and sign the National Accord on Acid Rain Abatement. They are still defying the commitment that they made in 1984 and 1985, and even in 1986, and because of sheer neglect on the part of this Government it allows the Americans to criticize us for not maintaining our side of the commitment that by 1994 we will cut our sulphur dioxide pollution by 50 per cent.
Although it is belated, I welcome the conversion of the Minister to the notion that we must do something in the United States, and that he must go to Washington and make important visits to those who need to be convinced that Canada has a case. However, this conversion comes in the fourth year of this administration.
It distresses me to learn about the intention of the Government to spend money on advertising in the United States. Will we complain to the United States about how hard done by we are? That has been done many times. I do not think it will get
Adjournment Debate
us anywhere to complain about that. The Americans may be sympathetic, but they will not be moved by that type of argument. They will be moved by arguments that deal with their economic interest and their own economy.
I wish to ask the Parliamentary Secretary why the Government is not prepared to prepare a case that would explain to the Americans the cost to them of not proceeding with action in cutting air pollution from their coal fired plants. What will be the cost to the United States for not acting and removing those poisonous gases which are inflicting damage to their buildings, structures, lakes, forests, and agriculture? In addition to the damage they are doing to us, the Americans would be very sensitive to a study that points out the economic damage inflicted on their economy by their pollution.
Finally, I wish to ask the Parliamentary Secretary why the Government at this stage, in the fourth year of its mandate, is not putting together data and information required to prepare a bill that would be submitted to Washington for the yearly damage to our economy that is caused by their pollution. We could start with the bill from the producers of maple syrup in Quebec and Ontario. I am sure that they would be more than glad to quantify the damage caused to the maple forests that is provoked and caused by transboundary pollution from south of the border. It is estimated to be more than $1 million a year.
These are some of the questions that I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will address in his reply. I am looking forward to his statement.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan Schellenberger (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) raises an important issue. The resolution of this problem is a priority of the Government.
Resolution requires action both domestically and bilaterally. We are working with the provincial Governments and with the Canadian industry to ensure the implementation of an effective acid rain control program. To date, more than 90 per cent of the necessary emission reductions are in regulatory or program form.
Bilaterally we are pressing the United States for early reductions in U.S. emissions affecting Canada. Over the last few years we have seen some progress in the United States.
In 1986, we saw U.S. President Reagan acknowledge the acid rain problem. This represented a breakthrough in the thinking of the U.S. administration. At the same time we saw the President take a step toward solving the acid rain problem by endorsing the Report of the Special Envoys on Acid Rain.
Again, in March 1987, we saw the President propose a clean coal technology program and a bilateral panel to oversee its implementation. None of us has been impressed with either the pace or the extent of the action of the U.S. administration on acid rain. However, as U.S. Senator George Mitchell, a

September 29, 1987
Adjournment Debate
proponent of acid rain control legislation, has said, "none of this would have happened without the unrelenting pressure of the Canadian Government".
Our message to the Americans is clear and unequivocal. Canada is putting its house in order with regard to acid rain. We expect the United States to respect its obligations as our neighbour and to control the contribution its sources are making to Canada's acid rain problem.
Based on scientific information, the resolution of the acid rain problem depends on the United States cutting the
transboundary flow of sulphur dioxide to two million tonnes per year. We intend to continue to convey that strong message to the Government of the United States.
